0.title: A Farewell Letter from the Rock
0.overview:
Second Peter is the apostle's last will and testament. Writing in the shadow of his own death — 'the putting off of my body will be soon, as our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me' (1:14; cf. John 21:18–19) — Peter addresses a church under pressure from false teachers who have crept inside the community, twisted Paul's letters, and weaponized a crude uniformitarianism against the hope of Christ's return. The letter's three movements answer three threats: the erosion of moral seriousness (ch. 1: grow in the divine nature), the corruption of doctrine by immoral teachers (ch. 2: their condemnation is certain), and the mocking of eschatological hope (ch. 3: the Day is coming and it will be unlike anything the world has seen).

The letter's authorship is the most contested in the NT canon. The vocabulary differs sharply from 1 Peter, and Origen already noted that some doubted it. Eusebius placed it among the antilegomena — letters known but disputed. Yet the arguments for Petrine authorship are substantial: the self-identification is unusually specific (Simeon Peter, v.1; the eyewitness claim of vv.16–18; the reference to a prior letter in 3:1); a forger who fabricates this much personal detail is extraordinarily bold. The vocabulary difference most likely reflects a different secretary — 1 Peter was written dia Silouanou (through Silvanus, 1 Pet 5:12), while 2 Peter's quite different style may reflect Peter writing without that help, or with another. The church ultimately recognized it as canonical, and its theological weight — the virtue chain, the transfiguration testimony, the patience of God, the new creation — fully justifies that recognition.

The relationship to Jude is unavoidable: 2 Peter 2 and Jude share extensive material (the angels who sinned, Sodom and Gomorrah, the Balaam archetype, waterless clouds, the scoffers of the last days). The majority of scholars believe Peter used Jude (not the reverse), which, if correct, places 2 Peter after Jude and in the mid-to-late 60s AD — consistent with Peter's death under Nero (c. 64–68 AD). Peter does not merely copy Jude; he develops, expands, and re-focuses the material for a church whose crisis has moved from external pressure to internal corruption.

1.title: Partakers of the Divine Nature
1.text: <sup>1</sup>Simeon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, To those who have obtained a faith of equal standing with ours by the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ:<sup>2</sup>May grace and peace be multiplied to you in the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord.<sup>3</sup>His divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness, through the knowledge of him who called us to his own glory and excellence,<sup>4</sup>by which he has granted to us his precious and very great promises, so that through them you may become partakers of the divine nature, having escaped from the corruption that is in the world because of sinful desire.<sup>5</sup>For this very reason, make every effort to supplement your faith with virtue, and virtue with knowledge,<sup>6</sup>and knowledge with self-control, and self-control with steadfastness, and steadfastness with godliness,<sup>7</sup>and godliness with brotherly affection, and brotherly affection with love.<sup>8</sup>For if these qualities are yours and are increasing, they keep you from being ineffective or unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ.<sup>9</sup>For whoever lacks these qualities is so nearsighted that he is blind, having forgotten that he was cleansed from his former sins.<sup>10</sup>Therefore, brothers, be all the more diligent to confirm your calling and election, for if you practice these qualities you will never fall.<sup>11</sup>For in this way there will be richly provided for you an entrance into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.<sup>12</sup>Therefore I intend always to remind you of these qualities, though you know them and are established in the truth that you have.<sup>13</sup>I think it right, as long as I am in this body, to stir you up by way of reminder,<sup>14</sup>since I know that the putting off of my body will be soon, as our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me.<sup>15</sup>And I will make every effort so that after my departure you may be able at any time to recall these things.<sup>16</sup>For we did not follow cleverly devised myths when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty.<sup>17</sup>For when he received honor and glory from God the Father, and the voice was borne to him by the Majestic Glory, "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased,"<sup>18</sup>we ourselves heard this very voice borne from heaven, for we were with him on the holy mountain.<sup>19</sup>And we have the prophetic word more fully confirmed, to which you will do well to pay attention as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts,<sup>20</sup>knowing this first of all, that no prophecy of Scripture comes from someone's own interpretation.<sup>21</sup>For no prophecy was ever produced by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.
1.overview:
Chapter 1 lays the foundation. God’s power has already given believers everything they need for life and godliness (v. 3). On that gift rests the command: make every effort to add to your faith, and so confirm your calling (vv. 5, 10). Gift first, then effort: that is the grammar of grace.

The second half grounds Peter’s message in two witnesses that agree: the apostles saw Christ’s glory at the transfiguration, and the prophetic Scriptures, spoken by men carried along by the Holy Spirit, point to the same Christ and his coming day.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Divine Power and Precious Promises
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter writes to believers whose faith is of equal value to his own. God’s power has given them everything for life and godliness, and his promises make them sharers in his holy nature. So they make every effort to grow from faith to love, and so confirm their calling.
verseByVerse.theology:
Partakers of the Divine Nature

God’s power has already granted everything needed for life and godliness. Sharing the divine nature means sharing his holiness, not becoming God, and growth in the qualities of verses 5–7 is how a believer confirms his calling.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter told readers who had seen nothing that their faith was of equal standing with his.

Now: When growth stalls, look first for a memory of forgiveness that has grown dim (v. 9).

verseByVerse.quote: Simeon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, To those who have obtained a faith of equal standing with ours by the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ: May grace and peace be multiplied to you in the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 2 Peter 1 lays the foundation for resisting false teachers: true knowledge of Christ, growing character, and the sure word of Scripture. God’s power has given us everything for life and godliness, and by his promises we share the divine nature (vv. 1–4). So believers add to faith a chain of virtues ending in love, and so confirm their calling (vv. 5–11). Facing death, Peter reminds them that the message is no myth: he saw Christ’s majesty on the mountain, and Scripture came from men carried along by the Holy Spirit (vv. 12–21).

The setting. Peter’s farewell letter, written as he expected to die soon (1:14), probably from Rome around AD 64–68, shortly before, as early tradition holds, his martyrdom under Nero. (On its authorship, see the textual note below.) It addresses the same churches as 1 Peter (3:1). Its concern is false teachers within the churches who denied Christ’s return and lived immorally (chapters 2–3; compare Jude). The first letter was written to Christians suffering from outside; this one to Christians endangered from inside. Persecution can kill the body, but false teaching can empty a church while leaving its building full, and Peter, with the executioner not far off, judged it the greater danger.

Simeon Peter. Not Simon but Symeōn, the old Hebrew form (some manuscripts, and the KJV, read Simon), used of Peter elsewhere only by James (Acts 15:14). Then both names together: the one he was born with and the one Jesus gave him, Petros, rock. A man writing his last letter signs it with his whole history: the fisherman who sank in the lake and swore he did not know the man; and the rock, which he never became by his own strength but was made by the One who named him.

A servant and apostle. Servant first, doulos, a slave, and apostle second. The man who once argued about who was the greatest now introduces himself as the property of another. Because he is Christ’s slave, he can speak with Christ’s authority: an apostle is a man sent with a message that is not his, and the only way to carry such a message faithfully is to have no ambitions of your own for it.

A faith of equal standing. Obtained, lachousin, is a word for receiving by lot: faith is an allotment, a gift, not a prize won (Ephesians 2:8). Of equal standing, isotimon, means of the same value. Peter had seen the Transfiguration and will describe it in fifteen verses; he tells readers who have seen nothing, probably mostly Gentiles who never heard Jesus’ voice, that their faith is of exactly equal worth to his. There is no first-class and second-class Christianity.

My faith feels nothing like an apostle’s. How can it be equal? Because faith is not valued by its strength but by its object. A weak hand and a strong hand receive the same gift; a trembling faith in a mighty Christ saves as surely as a bold one. What is equal is not your feelings, your knowledge or your record, but the Christ you hold and the righteousness given to you. Thomas, who doubted, and the thief, who believed in his last hours, received the same Saviour as Peter. So do not measure your standing by comparing your faith with other people’s. Measure it by whom you are trusting, and grow from there.

Our God and Savior Jesus Christ. In Greek a single article governs both nouns, a construction that normally marks them as one person. Peter calls Jesus God directly, as Paul does in Titus 2:13. The same construction in 1:11, 2:20 and 3:18 (“our Lord and Savior”) plainly names one person. It is one of the New Testament’s clearest statements of Christ’s deity, and it stands at the front door of a letter written against men who denied the Master who bought them (2:1). Righteousness, dikaiosynē, carries two shades together: God’s fairness in giving the same faith to all, Jew and Gentile, apostle and newcomer; and the righteousness of Christ himself, by which believers are justified. Justification is God counting a person righteous because Christ’s righteousness is credited to the one who trusts him (Romans 4:5). The faith is equal because the righteousness is his, and it is not divided into larger and smaller portions.

Grace and peace be multiplied. Not merely given but multiplied, as in 1 Peter 1:2, because the God who gives grace does not run short of it. Grace is God’s free favour; peace is what it produces: reconciliation with God and rest within.

In the knowledge of God. The letter’s key word: knowledge, epignōsis, is full, personal, experiential knowledge, the knowing that belongs to a relationship rather than a library. It appears four times in this short letter (1:2, 3, 8; 2:20), and it is Peter’s answer to the false teachers, who were probably offering knowledge of another kind: secret, superior, liberating from ordinary morality. Peter answers not by despising knowledge but by naming the true knowledge of God in Christ.

Is this knowledge just a matter of learning doctrine? No, though it is never less than that. You cannot know a person while being wrong about who he is, so true doctrine matters. But Peter means knowing God the way a child knows his father: trusting him, hearing him, walking with him, and growing in that acquaintance over years. It comes through his word, through prayer, through the worship and fellowship of his people, and through obeying him and finding him faithful. A man can know a great deal about God and not know him; a simple believer may know little theology and know him truly. The aim is both: a mind that is accurate and a heart that is personally acquainted.

Textual note. 2 Peter was one of the most disputed books in the early church: early church writers report that some doubted it, and noticed that its style differs from 1 Peter. Most modern scholars think a follower wrote it in Peter’s name after his death, pointing to that difference of style, to its heavy use of the material in Jude, to its mention of Paul’s letters as a collection counted with the Scriptures (3:15–16), and to the complaint that the fathers have fallen asleep (3:4). These are real questions, and honest scholars weigh them differently. On the other side, the letter plainly claims to be from Peter, refers to the Transfiguration as an eyewitness (vv. 16–18), mentions Jesus’ prediction of Peter’s death (v. 14), and refers to a previous letter (3:1); the early church rejected writings it knew to be falsely attributed, and, after careful consideration, received this one. Differences of style may be due to a different secretary or none (Silvanus helped with 1 Peter, 1 Peter 5:12) and to a different subject. The question cannot be settled by proof either way. This commentary receives the letter as Peter’s, as the church long has, and as Scripture.

What it does not mean. “Equal standing” does not mean all believers have the same apostolic authority. It means the same saving faith, equally precious to God. Equality of faith is not equality of office (3:2).

On a Tuesday. If you know someone who feels like a second-class believer, the new convert with a chaotic past, the believer who cannot pray aloud, tell them what Peter told his readers: your faith is as precious as his.
verseByVerse.note: Peter’s farewell letter, written as he expected to die soon (1:14), probably from Rome in the mid 60s AD. “Simeon” is the Hebrew form of his name.

verseByVerse.quote: His divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness, through the knowledge of him who called us to his own glory and excellence, by which he has granted to us his precious and very great promises, so that through them you may become partakers of the divine nature, having escaped from the corruption that is in the world because of sinful desire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His divine power has granted. Granted, dedōrēmenēs, is perfect tense: has given, and it remains ours. Not supplied in instalments, but given in full. This sentence closes a door before the false teachers can open it. If everything necessary has been provided, then no supplementary knowledge is on offer, and anyone promising a further instalment is selling something that does not exist.

If I have everything, why do I feel I am lacking so much? Because having and using are different things. A man may inherit a great house and live in one room of it, cold and hungry, because he has never opened the other doors. Peter does not say you already feel complete or behave perfectly; he says the resources are yours. What you lack is not a new gift but growth in using the one you have: knowing Christ better, trusting his promises more, and practising what he has already made possible. That is why the next verses call for effort. So when someone offers you a secret, a second blessing, a technique or a special experience that will finally make the Christian life work, you may answer kindly: I have been given all things in Christ, and I need to know him better, not something besides him.

Him who called us. Called, kalesantos, is God’s effectual call: not an invitation merely issued and left to us, but the summons that creates what it commands, as Jesus’ voice brought Lazarus out of the tomb.

His own glory and excellence. Glory, doxa, is the radiance of who he is. Excellence, aretē, is moral goodness, the word of the excellencies of the one who called us out of darkness into his marvellous light (1 Peter 2:9). The Greek can mean that God called us by his glory and excellence, drawn by his beauty as Peter himself was drawn when he fell at Jesus’ knees in the boat, or that he called us to share them. Probably both. He calls us into the very thing he is.

Precious and very great promises. Precious, timia, is his recurring word (1 Peter 1:7, 19). What promises? Forgiveness, the gift of the Spirit, eternal life, Christ’s return, the new heavens and new earth in which righteousness dwells (3:4, 9, 13). They are given, not dangled: God has bound himself by his word, and every one of his promises finds its Yes in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20).

Partakers of the divine nature. Partakers, koinōnoi, is the word for business partners in Luke 5:10, where James and John were Simon’s partners in the fishing. Through God’s promises believers share in God’s own moral character and life: his holiness, love and goodness. This is the new birth and union with Christ (John 15:4–5; Colossians 3:10). It does not mean human beings become God (see below), nor is it a poetic exaggeration: God’s own life is truly in his people. The Holy Spirit lives in every believer (Romans 8:9), and he gives you desires that are God’s own, so that you begin to love what God loves, holiness, truth and his people, and to hate what he hates. You remain a creature, but you are no longer only what you were.

He shared ours. The way into this sharing runs through the incarnation. Since the children share in flesh and blood, Hebrews says, he himself likewise partook of the same things, that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death (Hebrews 2:14). The Son took our nature, without ceasing to be God, so that in union with him we might receive his life, without ceasing to be creatures. Christians share the divine nature only because the divine Son first, and freely, shared the human one.

How can a promise make me share God’s nature? Because God’s promises are not information about a distant future; they are the means by which the Spirit unites us to Christ now. When you believe God’s promise that your sins are forgiven, you are freed from guilt and drawn to love him. When you believe that Christ is coming and you will be like him (1 John 3:2–3), you begin to purify yourself as he is pure. A promise believed changes what you want. That is how the new nature grows: not by striving to become divine, but by trusting what God has said, until his character is reproduced in yours.

Having escaped from the corruption. Escaped, apophygontes, means fled, as from a burning building. Corruption, phthora, is moral rot; and the world’s rot comes from disordered desire (James 1:14–15). The clause defines the divine nature by its opposite: holiness, not divinity. Peter will use the same word of the false teachers, who promise freedom while they themselves are slaves of corruption (2:19). There are only two directions: toward God’s life, or toward the rot.

Where Christians differ: do believers become divine? Eastern Orthodoxy teaches theosis or deification, in which believers progressively become gods by grace; Orthodox theologians themselves insist that believers share God’s energies, his life and activity, never his essence, so the difference from Reformed teaching is real but narrower than it sounds. Some modern movements go further and teach that believers become little gods. This commentary’s view: Believers share in God’s moral nature (his holiness, love and life) through union with Christ by the Spirit, but they never share in his essence, his deity, or his incommunicable attributes like omnipotence or omniscience. The Creator-creature distinction is never erased. We become like God in character, not God in being (1 John 3:2; 2 Corinthians 3:18).

On a Tuesday. Take one promise of God and carry it through the day. If you are anxious, his promise never to leave you (Hebrews 13:5); if you are tempted, his promise of a way of escape (1 Corinthians 10:13); if you are guilty, his promise to forgive the one who confesses (1 John 1:9). When the desire that rots presses on you, answer it with what God has said.

For worship. God has not given us a starter kit and left us to complete the set. He has given everything, by his own divine power, and the gift remains. We were rotting in the world’s decay, and he brought us out. He will not make us gods, but he has made us his children, partakers of the life that has no end.

verseByVerse.quote: For this very reason, make every effort to supplement your faith with virtue, and virtue with knowledge, and knowledge with self-control, and self-control with steadfastness, and steadfastness with godliness, and godliness with brotherly affection, and brotherly affection with love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this very reason, make every effort. Because God has given you everything (vv. 3–4). Make every effort, spoudēn pasan pareisenenkantes, is literally bringing in all diligence alongside: God has brought everything; you bring your diligence beside it. Grace is not opposed to effort; it is opposed to earning (Philippians 2:12–13). A man who has been given a farm does not earn it by ploughing, but he will certainly plough.

Supplement your faith with virtue. The verb, epichorēgēsate, is the chorēgos word, of the wealthy citizen who funded a festival chorus lavishly (1 Peter 4:11). Then eight qualities in a chain, each growing out of the last, on the ground of faith. The first quality built on it is virtue, aretē, moral excellence, the same word used of God in verse 3.

Knowledge. Gnōsis here is understanding and practical wisdom: knowing God’s will and how to apply it. Goodness without understanding blunders (Romans 10:2).

Self-control. Enkrateia is self-mastery, literally holding oneself in. Knowing what is right settles nothing until the appetites are governed. The false teachers had knowledge, or claimed it, without self-control (2:10–14), and Peter describes where that ends.

Steadfastness. Hypomonē is endurance, remaining under weight (James 1:3–4). It is self-control extended over time. Anyone can resist a temptation once. Steadfastness is resisting it on the four hundredth day, when the novelty of the fight has gone and the pressure has not.

Godliness. Eusebeia is reverence for God shown in life. A Stoic could have admired the qualities so far; godliness makes them Christian: everything done before God’s face, for his sake.

Brotherly affection. Philadelphia is family love for fellow believers: warmth, loyalty, enjoyment of one another, as children of the same Father. Godliness that does not love God’s children is not godliness (1 John 4:20).

Love. Agapē is self-giving love that reaches past the family to everyone, including enemies, the crown of the list (1 Corinthians 13:13; Colossians 3:14). The last link is the one that looks most like Christ, who loved his own and also prayed for those who crucified him.

Is this effort not a kind of legalism? No. Legalism is effort to earn God’s favour or to add to Christ’s work. Peter’s effort springs from favour already given: because God has granted you everything, make every effort. The difference is the difference between a slave labouring to buy his freedom and a son working in his father’s fields. Both may sweat. Only one does it from rest. If you notice that your effort has become anxious, proud or joyless, the remedy is not to stop trying but to go back to verses 3–4 and remember what you have been given. There is a quieter danger too. A list of virtues can become a self-improvement project, pursued so that you can admire yourself or be admired. Peter’s chain guards against that at both ends: it begins with faith, which only receives, and ends with love, which gives itself away.

Must I master these qualities one at a time, in order? No. Peter is not describing a staircase where you finish one step before you begin the next. The links grow together, each strengthening the others, like branches on one tree. The order shows how they depend on one another: knowledge guides goodness, self-control keeps knowledge honest, endurance makes self-control last. But a young believer shows something of all of them from the start, and the oldest saint is still growing in every one.

What does adding self-control actually look like? Start with one appetite that rules you more than it should: food, the phone, anger, spending, sleep, lust. Decide in advance, in the light of God’s word, what obedience looks like there. Remove what feeds it where you can. Tell a trusted believer and ask him to ask you. When you fail, confess it at once, receive forgiveness, and go again the same day. Self-control is not gritted teeth alone; it is the Spirit’s fruit (Galatians 5:23), and it grows as you rely on him in specific, repeated choices.

On a Tuesday. Ask someone who knows you well which link they see missing in you, and then be specific: not I will be more loving, but I will visit, phone or help this person, whom I have been avoiding.

For worship. Look at the chain and see a portrait. Faith resting wholly on the Father, goodness without a stain, knowledge of the Father’s will so perfect that he did always what pleased him, self-control in the wilderness when he was hungry, steadfastness all the way to the cross, godliness that said not my will but yours, affection for his brothers, and love for his enemies. Every link was first in Christ. And the God who called us by that excellence will reproduce it in us, until the family likeness is complete.

verseByVerse.quote: For if these qualities are yours and are increasing, they keep you from being ineffective or unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. For whoever lacks these qualities is so nearsighted that he is blind, having forgotten that he was cleansed from his former sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yours and increasing. Increasing, pleonazonta, means abounding. Peter assumes growth is the normal state, and that a static Christian life is already a warning sign. A tree that has not grown for years is either very old or dead.

Ineffective or unfruitful. Ineffective, argous, is literally idle, like the workers in the marketplace (Matthew 20:3). Unfruitful, akarpous, is barren. Peter is not saying these qualities earn knowledge, but that without them a man’s knowing goes nowhere. You may hold the doctrine accurately and be entirely unproductive in it, like a field with the best soil in the county that nobody has sown.

So nearsighted that he is blind. The word, myōpazōn, gives us myopic. The man sees what is right in front of him perfectly well, this week, this appetite, this grievance, this pay rise. What he cannot see is anything at a distance: eternity, the judgement seat, the coming kingdom, the souls of people around him. Short-sightedness, left alone, becomes blindness, the false teachers’ disease exactly. They will scoff at the coming of the Lord (3:4), because they cannot see further than their own desires.

Having forgotten that he was cleansed. The root: forgotten is literally having taken forgetfulness (lēthēn labōn), as though he had picked it up and put it on. Cleansed, katharismos, is Christ’s purification for sins (Hebrews 1:3). He has lost sight of his own cleansing: not necessarily lost the cleansing, but the memory of it. A Christian who forgets what he was forgiven has no fuel for growth, because gratitude is the engine of the whole chain in verses 5–7. When growth has stopped, look for a memory gone dim, not a missing technique. The woman in Luke 7 who washed Jesus’ feet with her tears loved much because she knew she had been forgiven much.

I feel stuck and fruitless. Am I a Christian at all? The fact that it troubles you is a good sign; the man Peter describes is not troubled, he is drowsy. Begin where Peter puts the problem: with memory. Go back to the cross and look again at what your sins cost and how freely they were washed away. Read a Gospel slowly, or Psalm 103, or Isaiah 53. Confess the specific sins that have choked growth. Then take one step of obedience in one of the qualities of verses 5–7. Fruit grows slowly and is often seen first by others, so ask a mature believer what they see. And do not judge your whole standing by one dry season; judge it by where you run.

On a Tuesday. Before you sleep tonight, lift your eyes past the next week to the day you will see Christ. Then remember one specific sin you have been forgiven, and thank him for it by name. The memory will do more for your growth than a new resolution.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, brothers, be all the more diligent to confirm your calling and election, for if you practice these qualities you will never fall. For in this way there will be richly provided for you an entrance into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be all the more diligent. Be diligent, spoudasate, echoes verse 5, and all the more raises it. And brothers, the only time in the letter: after the warning, a brother pleading with brothers.

To confirm your calling and election. The trouble this sentence causes dissolves when we ask who is being confirmed to whom. Confirm, bebaian poieisthai, means to make firm, make sure; a related word was a legal term for ratifying a contract or guaranteeing a sale. Calling is God’s effectual call; election, eklogē, is God’s eternal choice. Peter does not say make God’s election secure: that is not in anyone’s power. Calling is mentioned first because it is how we come to know our election: we see the call in time and learn from it the choice made before time. We cannot make our election more certain to God; it is fixed. But we can make it more certain to ourselves, by growing in the qualities of verses 5–7, which are the evidence of genuine faith. The fruit does not create the root; it demonstrates it: not works establishing salvation, but works establishing certainty.

The kindness in it. A Christian anxious about whether he is truly God’s is not told to search his memory for a decisive moment, nor to look inward for a feeling. He is told to look for growth in ordinary character, which is visible, and which other people can see too. Election is not a locked room to be broken into by speculation.

You will never fall. Practise, poiountes, is present tense: keep doing. Never fall, ou mē ptaisēte pote, is a strong double negative: you will certainly never, ever stumble. It is not a promise of sinlessness but of not coming to ruin: you will never fall away, never be lost. We still stumble in lesser ways every day; but Christ obeyed perfectly in our place, his righteousness is counted as ours (Romans 5:19), and so our faltering practice is accepted for his sake.

Does if you practise these qualities mean that perseverance depends on our effort? The qualities are the fruit of the divine power that has given us all we need (v. 3), and by them believers confirm their calling, show it to be real, to themselves and others. Those who belong to Christ are kept by him (John 10:28–29); diligence is the way his keeping works out in our lives, not a rival to it.

Richly provided. Plousiōs epichorēgēthēsetai is the chorēgos word again, as in verse 5, and now the direction reverses. They were told to supply these qualities lavishly; God will lavishly supply their entrance. Entrance, eisodos, is a welcome, like a general’s through the city gates. Not a man scraping in as the door shuts, smelling of smoke (1 Corinthians 3:15), but a son coming home to a feast, into the kingdom no false teacher can scoff away.

Of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. The same construction as verse 1: one person, Lord and Saviour. The way in is his doing. He entered once for all into the holy places, not by the blood of goats and calves but by his own blood, securing an eternal redemption (Hebrews 9:12), and he told his disciples he was going to prepare a place for them and would come again to take them to himself (John 14:2–3). The entrance is richly provided because the King has already gone through the gate ahead of his people, and he is the one standing at it.

Where Christians differ: can I know I am elect? Some fear election makes assurance impossible: how can I know if God chose me? Others think assurance comes only by special revelation. This commentary’s view: Believers can and should have assurance of their election. It is grounded first in God’s promises in Christ, received by faith; it is confirmed by the Spirit’s inner witness (Romans 8:16) and by the fruit of a godly life (1 John 2:3; 3:14). Election is not a cause for anxiety but for confidence: those who trust Christ and grow in godliness may know they are chosen (1 Thessalonians 1:4–5). And the elect will persevere: they will never fall.

Can a true Christian fall away and be lost? No. Those God has chosen and called he keeps, and none of them will be snatched out of Christ’s hand (John 10:28–29; Romans 8:30; Philippians 1:6). True believers can fall into serious sin for a time, as Peter himself did on the night he denied the Lord, and they may lose the joy of their salvation and come under the Father’s discipline. But they are brought back, because Christ prays for them as he prayed for Peter (Luke 22:32). Those who abandon the faith altogether show that they never truly belonged (1 John 2:19). Many faithful Christians in the Arminian and Wesleyan traditions, who hold that a believer can freely turn away and be lost, read the warnings of Scripture differently, and they rightly take those warnings seriously; this commentary holds the Reformed view of perseverance because of promises like John 10:28–29, while honouring them as brothers. So the promise of this verse is not a reason to relax but a reason to keep going without fear.

What if I look and cannot see the fruit? First, look at Christ before you look at yourself. Assurance rests first on his promise to receive all who come (John 6:37), not on your inspection. Second, look honestly but not morbidly: fruit is often small, slow and more visible to others than to you. Do you trust him? Do you want to obey him? Do you grieve over sin? Do you love his people? Third, if you find almost nothing, do not sit down in despair. Go to Christ now as a sinner, and begin to obey. The way to confirm your calling is not endless self-examination but present faith and diligence.

For worship. Before the world was made he chose us, and in time his voice found us and called us by name. He keeps those he calls, so that the one who stumbled on a dark night by a courtyard fire could write, half a lifetime later, you will never fall.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–21 — Eyewitnesses and the Prophetic Word
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Facing the death Jesus foretold, Peter keeps reminding his readers of what they already know. Their faith rests on two witnesses that agree: the apostles who saw Christ’s majesty on the mountain, and the prophetic word, spoken by men whom the Holy Spirit carried along.
verseByVerse.theology:
Carried Along

Prophecy did not come from the prophet’s own interpretation. Men spoke from God as the Holy Spirit carried them along: fully human, and fully God’s word.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter wrote knowing his death was near, and arranged for his readers to remember.

Now: Scripture is a lamp in a dark place, enough light until the day dawns.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I intend always to remind you of these qualities, though you know them and are established in the truth that you have. I think it right, as long as I am in this body, to stir you up by way of reminder, since I know that the putting off of my body will be soon, as our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me. And I will make every effort so that after my departure you may be able at any time to recall these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I intend always to remind you. Remind, hypomimnēskein, means keep reminding, and it is a key theme of the letter (1:12, 13, 15; 3:1–2). They know these things, and he will go on saying them anyway, against the appetite for novelty the false teachers exploited. Most of what a congregation needs is not new information but the same truth said again, because knowing a thing and having it present to you are different states. A man knows he loves his wife; he still needs to remember it at six o’clock on a tiring evening.

Established in the truth. Established, estērigmenous, is perfect tense: settled and still standing. It is the word Jesus used to Peter on the night of the denial: when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers (Luke 22:32). The man who could not stand firm for a night is spending his last days making others firm.

As long as I am in this body. Body, skēnōma, is literally tent, and the image governs the paragraph. A tent is struck when the journey moves on (2 Corinthians 5:1–4). Stir you up, diegeirein, means to wake someone; it is used of the disciples waking Jesus in the storm (Luke 8:24) (compare 3:1). His model of ministry is not filling empty heads but waking drowsy ones.

Is it not boring to hear the same things again and again? Only if you think the purpose of hearing is to collect information. Food is the same every day and nobody calls bread boring; we need it again because we used up the last meal. The gospel is like that. Yesterday’s assurance does not carry today’s temptation; the truth must be brought fresh to a heart that leaks. A good preacher will find new ways to say old things, but you should be suspicious of any teacher whose main selling point is that he has something nobody has heard before. In Christian truth, what is new is seldom true, and what is true is never stale to a hungry soul.

The putting off of my body. Apothesis is laying aside, as one takes off clothing. Death lays aside the body, not the person, and Peter speaks of it calmly.

As our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me. Peter knows he is going to die because he was told. On the beach, after the third question about love, Jesus said that when he was old others would stretch out his hands and lead him where he did not want to go, and John adds that this indicated the kind of death by which he would glorify God (John 21:18–19). The stretched-out hands meant crucifixion, and early tradition says Peter was crucified in Rome under Nero. He was told it on the morning of his restoration, in the conversation in which Jesus said, follow me, and he has been following ever since, toward that death, with his eyes open.

After my departure. Departure, exodos, is the word Luke uses for what Moses and Elijah spoke of on the mountain: Jesus’ own death, his departure which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31). Peter had heard that conversation. His death is an exodus, behind the Lord who went first. And he is not settling affairs but arranging for them to remember after he has gone. He may mean this letter itself, or perhaps Mark’s Gospel, which early tradition says records Peter’s preaching.

How should a Christian think about his own death? As Peter did: as the folding of a tent and an exodus, not as the end. To be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8), at once, not in a sleep and not in a purgatory, but with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23). We may still fear dying, the process, the pain, the parting, and that is no sin; even Jesus was in anguish in the garden. But death itself has lost its sting (1 Corinthians 15:55–57). So use the time well. Peter’s question was not how long have I left? but what will they remember when I am gone? Ask the same.

On a Tuesday. Who will remember Christ better because of you: your children, a younger believer, a friend? A few lines telling one of them what Christ has been to you may outlast much else you leave, and you need not be dying to write them.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus had told Peter how he would die.

verseByVerse.quote: For we did not follow cleverly devised myths when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty. For when he received honor and glory from God the Father, and the voice was borne to him by the Majestic Glory, "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased," we ourselves heard this very voice borne from heaven, for we were with him on the holy mountain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not cleverly devised myths. Cleverly devised, sesophismenois, means made up. The false teachers were evidently saying that Christ’s coming was a tale to frighten people into good behaviour. Peter’s reply is historical. Myths were set in a timeless past no one could check; the gospel is not like that. It names a governor, a city, a mountain, and men who were there.

The power and coming. Dynamin kai parousian probably means his powerful coming: the second coming, which the false teachers denied (3:4). Parousia was used of a king’s state visit. The apostles had already seen a preview of it.

Eyewitnesses of his majesty. The word for eyewitnesses, epoptai, was used in the mystery religions for those admitted to the highest grade of initiation: those who had seen. Peter takes a word from the cults, with their secret rites and private visions, and applies it to something that happened on a mountain in daylight before three fishermen. Majesty, megaleiotēs, is the word used when the crowds were astonished at the majesty of God in Jesus’ healing (Luke 9:43). At the Transfiguration, Peter saw the King’s face as it will be seen on the day he comes.

Honor and glory from God the Father. Peter is describing the Transfiguration (Matthew 17:1–8; Mark 9:2–8; Luke 9:28–36), and he was one of three men there: the honour of the Father’s word, and the glory of the Son’s own radiance shining through.

The Majestic Glory. A reverent way of naming God, perhaps the bright cloud of his presence that filled the tabernacle, come down again on the mountain. Matthew tells us that when the disciples heard the voice they fell on their faces, terrified (Matthew 17:6). Holiness that near is not cosy. Then Jesus came and touched them and told them to rise and not be afraid (Matthew 17:7): the glory that flattens sinners belongs to the one who lifts them up.

My beloved Son. The Father’s declaration echoes Psalm 2:7 and Isaiah 42:1, and the words at Jesus’ baptism (Matthew 3:17). Peter does not describe the shining face or Moses and Elijah; he reports the voice, because the argument concerns testimony. The Father himself named his Son, King and Servant, and declared his delight in him.

On the holy mountain. The mountain was made holy by God’s presence as Sinai once was (tradition says Tabor; Hermon fits the Gospels well). And there is something moving in the restraint. Peter had wanted to build three shelters and stay, and had spoken without knowing what he was saying (Luke 9:33). He mentions none of that. Decades on he reports only what is admissible: we were there, and we heard.

Why does the Transfiguration prove that Christ will come again? Because it was the coming in miniature. Jesus had just said that some standing there would not taste death until they saw the Son of Man coming in his kingdom (Matthew 16:28), and six days later three of them did: the glory he will have when he comes was briefly uncovered before their eyes. The scoffers said the King would never come in power. Peter replies that he has already seen the King in his power. What was hidden for a moment on the mountain will be revealed to the whole world on the last day.

How do we know the apostles were not simply mistaken or lying? Consider what their testimony cost them. Men do not willingly die for what they know to be a lie, and Peter is writing under the shadow of crucifixion. Sincerity alone does not prove a thing true, but these men were not reporting a private belief: they claimed to have seen and heard for themselves, so they were in a position to know whether it was a lie. Some scholars think this letter was written by a follower after Peter’s death; even so, the Transfiguration does not rest on this letter alone, for three Gospels report it, written within living memory. Their accounts are sober, full of their own failures, written within living memory of the events, when others who were there could contradict them. And the testimony is not one man’s vision: three men on the mountain, and hundreds who saw the risen Christ (1 Corinthians 15:6). Christian faith is not a leap in the dark; it is trust in reliable witnesses, confirmed by the Spirit who opens our eyes to see that what they say is true.

Should I seek experiences of glory like Peter’s? No. Peter himself, having had the greatest experience a man could have, does not tell his readers to seek one. He points them in the next verse to the prophetic word. The Transfiguration was a unique moment given to chosen witnesses to found the church’s testimony, and it has been written down so that you may believe without seeing (John 20:29). God may give believers deep joy and a sense of his nearness, and we may thank him for it, but our faith rests on what happened and what is written, not on what we feel.

On a Tuesday. When someone dismisses the faith as a nice story, do not be rattled or defensive. Say plainly that Christianity stands or falls on events witnessed by named men, and offer to read one of the Gospels with them.
verseByVerse.note: The “holy mountain” is the Mount of Transfiguration, where Peter, James and John saw Jesus’ glory.

verseByVerse.quote: And we have the prophetic word more fully confirmed, to which you will do well to pay attention as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prophetic word more fully confirmed. The prophetic word is the Old Testament Scriptures as a whole, which prophesy Christ, including his coming in glory. More fully confirmed, bebaioteron, is from the same family as the word for confirming your calling (v. 10). Either the Transfiguration confirmed the prophecies, or the Scriptures are even more reliable than Peter’s experience, which fits verses 20–21: Scripture comes from God himself. Either way Peter is not belittling what he saw, and his readers, who were not on the mountain and never would be, are told that what they hold in their hands is the firmest ground there is.

Is Scripture really more certain than seeing something with my own eyes? Yes, in this sense: eyes can be deceived, memories fade, and experiences need interpreting, but God’s written word does not change and cannot lie. Peter’s experience on the mountain was real, yet it lasted minutes, was seen by three men, and needed words from God to explain it. Scripture is God’s own permanent testimony, given for every believer in every age. So when an experience, a dream, an impression or a strong feeling seems to say one thing and Scripture says another, Scripture wins every time. That is not distrust of God’s work in us; it is trust in his clearest word to us.

You will do well to pay attention. Pay attention, prosechontes: hold the mind on it, as a sailor on a light.

A lamp shining in a dark place. Lamp, lychnos, is a small oil lamp. Dark place, auchmēros topos, is a dry, murky place where nothing grows: this world, and Scripture is the lamp (Psalm 119:105). A lamp is not the sun; it is enough to see the next few feet by. Peter is honest about how much light Scripture gives in this age: sufficient, and not yet daylight. We do not see everything. We see enough to walk.

Until the day dawns. The day of Christ’s return (Romans 13:12): the lamp is temporary, and a morning is coming.

The morning star. Phōsphoros, light-bearer, is the planet Venus, the last light before sunrise and the herald of it. It points to Christ himself, the bright morning star (Revelation 22:16) (Numbers 24:17). So the dawn is his coming, which is precisely what the false teachers were denying. In your hearts surprises: the Christ who will appear publicly will fill the heart with light, and believers will know him fully (1 Corinthians 13:12). Until then, we need the lamp of Scripture.

Does God still speak today apart from the Bible? This commentary holds that the gifts of new revelation, prophecy in the sense of authoritative words from God, ceased with the apostles, and that the canon of Scripture is closed (Hebrews 1:1–2; Jude 3). The reason is that the apostles and prophets were the church’s foundation, laid once (Ephesians 2:20), and a foundation is not laid again in every generation. Many dear brothers in Christ believe otherwise, and we hold our view with charity. But on the practical point there is wide agreement among Bible-believing Christians: Scripture is the lamp, sufficient for faith and life, and nothing that claims to be from God may add to it or contradict it. The Spirit does speak today, through the word he inspired, applying it to our hearts. If you want to hear God speak, open the Bible.

For worship. God has not left us in the dark. He lit a lamp and put it in our hands, and every page of it was shining toward one Person. One day the lamp will be set down, not because it failed, but because the Sun himself has come, and we shall see him whom we have loved without seeing.

verseByVerse.quote: knowing this first of all, that no prophecy of Scripture comes from someone's own interpretation. For no prophecy was ever produced by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Knowing this first of all. Above all, of first importance: before anything else about Scripture, know where it came from.

Someone’s own interpretation. Interpretation, epilysis, means explanation, the solving of something obscure. It is often taken to forbid private interpretation, but the subject is the origin of prophecy, not its later handling, and verse 21 explains verse 20 directly, beginning with for. Prophecy was not a gifted man’s insight into his times; the message came from God.

Never produced by the will of man. Produced, ēnechthē, means was carried. The negative is absolute: no prophet sat down and decided to write the word of God.

Men spoke from God. Two things held together. Men spoke: real people, with their own vocabulary, style and circumstances. Isaiah does not sound like Amos; Paul does not sound like John. (The KJV’s holy men of God spake follows later manuscripts; the earliest read men spoke from God, as most modern Bibles do.) And they spoke from God: the message originated with him.

Carried along by the Holy Spirit. The verb, pheromenoi, is a sailing word. It is used in Acts 27:15 and 17 of Paul’s ship, which had lost the power to steer and was driven before the wind. It is the verb of the voice borne from heaven (vv. 17–18). The men are not passive cargo; they are working the vessel, raising the sails. But the Spirit supplied the power and direction, and they arrived where the wind took them. This is the doctrine of inspiration: Scripture is God-breathed (2 Timothy 3:16), fully human and fully divine in its authorship, so that what Scripture says, God says. That is what is meant by calling Scripture inerrant: because God cannot lie (Numbers 23:19), whatever Scripture affirms is true, in its history as much as in its doctrine.

The Spirit of Christ in them. In his first letter Peter wrote that the Spirit of Christ in the prophets was indicating the sufferings of Christ and the subsequent glories (1 Peter 1:11). The wind that drove the prophetic ship blew from Christ and toward Christ. And Peter had learned to read the Scriptures that way from Christ himself, who on the road to Emmaus, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27), and who said plainly that Scripture cannot be broken (John 10:35). The Christian receives the Bible as the Lord Jesus received it: every word from God, and every page about him.

Where Christians differ: is Scripture fully inspired and without error? Some hold that Scripture is inspired only in its religious teaching, or that it contains human errors alongside divine truth. This commentary’s view: Because Scripture came from God through men carried along by the Spirit, it shares God’s truthfulness. It is inerrant in all that it affirms, infallible in its teaching, and sufficient for faith and life. The human authors were not mere typewriters; God used their personalities and research (Luke 1:1–4). But the Spirit so guided them that what they wrote is the very word of God (1 Thessalonians 2:13). Sola Scriptura: Scripture is the final authority over every tradition, experience and claim of revelation.

Does this mean that individual Christians may not interpret Scripture for themselves? Roman Catholic teaching has used the verse to argue that the church alone can interpret Scripture rightly. But Peter is speaking of where prophecy came from: not from the prophet’s own understanding, but from God, as men were carried along by the Spirit (v. 21). Every believer is to read and understand Scripture (Acts 17:11), humbly, in the fellowship of the church and with its teachers, testing all interpretation by Scripture itself.

Does this apply to the New Testament too? Yes. Peter speaks here of Old Testament prophecy, but in 3:2 he puts the commandment of the apostles alongside the prophets, and in 3:15–16 he places Paul’s letters among the other Scriptures. The same Spirit who carried the prophets was promised to the apostles to bring to their remembrance all that Jesus said and to guide them into all the truth (John 14:26; 16:13). The church did not make these books Scripture; it recognised the voice of its Shepherd in them. With the apostles’ writings the canon is complete, and no further book will be added (Jude 3; Hebrews 1:1–2).

What about the parts of the Bible that seem to contradict each other or science? Take them seriously, but humbly. Many apparent contradictions dissolve when we read carefully: different writers choosing different details, round numbers, the way ancient historians summarised speeches, or ordinary language describing what the eye sees, as we still say the sun rises. Some difficulties remain unsolved, and good Christian scholars have honestly said so. But a difficulty is not an error, and a great many supposed errors of a century ago have since been answered. When you meet one, keep reading, ask a mature teacher, consult a good commentary, and trust the God who cannot lie (Titus 1:2).

On a Tuesday. Before you open Scripture today, ask the Spirit who carried its writers to open your eyes. And when the word rebukes you, do not argue with the wind; set your sails by it.

1.theology:
The chapter’s great claim is that believers become partakers of the divine nature (v. 4). This is not deification in the sense of becoming God or merging into his being. It is moral sharing: through the Spirit and union with Christ, God’s own character, his holiness, patience, love and truthfulness, is formed in the believer. Calvin read it as a sharing in God’s qualities, not in his essence.

The doctrine of Scripture (vv. 20–21) is equally central. Scripture is God’s own word spoken through human writers whom the Spirit carried along, so their words carry his authority. That is why the prophetic word is more fully confirmed: the written word outlasts the eyewitness and is open to every believer.
1.examples:
The chain of virtues (vv. 5–7) speaks to Christians who stop at faith and see no need to grow. Peter’s answer: faith is the beginning, not the destination. The virtues are not the condition of salvation (they flow from faith, not to it) but the evidence that it is real and the direction of its growth.

The lamp (v. 19) helps believers who find Bible reading dry. You read it not because it is always exciting but because you are in a dark place and it is the lamp God has given.

2.title: The Anatomy of a False Teacher
2.text: <sup>1</sup>But false prophets also arose among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you, who will secretly bring in destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them, bringing upon themselves swift destruction.<sup>2</sup>And many will follow their sensuality, and because of them the way of truth will be blasphemed.<sup>3</sup>And in their greed they will exploit you with false words. Their condemnation from long ago is not idle, and their destruction is not asleep.<sup>4</sup>For if God did not spare angels when they sinned, but cast them into hell and committed them to chains of gloomy darkness to be kept until the judgment;<sup>5</sup>if he did not spare the ancient world, but preserved Noah, a herald of righteousness, with seven others, when he brought a flood upon the world of the ungodly;<sup>6</sup>if by turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes he condemned them to extinction, making them an example of what is going to happen to the ungodly;<sup>7</sup>and if he rescued righteous Lot, greatly distressed by the sensual conduct of the wicked<sup>8</sup>(for as that righteous man lived among them day after day, he was tormenting his righteous soul over their lawless deeds that he saw and heard);<sup>9</sup>then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials, and to keep the unrighteous under punishment until the day of judgment,<sup>10</sup>and especially those who indulge in the lust of defiling passion and despise authority. Bold and willful, they do not tremble as they blaspheme the glorious ones,<sup>11</sup>whereas angels, though greater in might and power, do not pronounce a blasphemous judgment against them before the Lord.<sup>12</sup>But these, like irrational animals, creatures of instinct, born to be caught and destroyed, blaspheming about matters of which they are ignorant, will also be destroyed in their destruction,<sup>13</sup>suffering wrong as the wage for their wrongdoing. They count it pleasure to revel in the daytime. They are blots and blemishes, reveling in their deceptions, while they feast with you.<sup>14</sup>They have eyes full of adultery, insatiable for sin. They entice unsteady souls. They have hearts trained in greed. Accursed children!<sup>15</sup>Forsaking the right way, they have gone astray. They have followed the way of Balaam, the son of Beor, who loved gain from wrongdoing,<sup>16</sup>but was rebuked for his own transgression; a speechless donkey spoke with human voice and restrained the prophet's madness.<sup>17</sup>These are waterless springs and mists driven by a storm. For them the gloom of utter darkness has been reserved.<sup>18</sup>For, speaking loud boasts of folly, they entice by sensual passions of the flesh those who are barely escaping from those who live in error.<sup>19</sup>They promise them freedom, but they themselves are slaves of corruption. For whatever overcomes a person, to that he is enslaved.<sup>20</sup>For if, after they have escaped the defilements of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and overcome, the last state has become worse for them than the first.<sup>21</sup>For it would have been better for them never to have known the way of righteousness than after knowing it to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them.<sup>22</sup>What the true proverb says has happened to them: "The dog returns to its own vomit, and the sow, after washing herself, returns to wallow in the mire."
2.overview:
Chapter 2 is Peter’s portrait of the false teacher: his method (slipping in quietly), his doctrine (denying the Master), his motive (greed) and his end (judgment already on its way). Three examples from history, the angels, the flood and Sodom, show that God judges the wicked and rescues the godly.

The key irony is v. 19: they promise freedom while they themselves are slaves of corruption. The test of a teacher is not the sophistication of his words but the shape of his life.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Arrival and Judgment of False Teachers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: False prophets troubled Israel, and false teachers will trouble the church. They deny the Master who bought them and exploit people for money. But history shows that the Lord knows how to rescue the godly and to hold the wicked for judgment.
verseByVerse.theology:
Righteous Lot

False teachers arise from within. God did not spare the angels, the ancient world or Sodom, yet he preserved Noah and rescued Lot. He knows how to rescue the godly and to hold the unrighteous for judgement.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Lot, compromised as he was, was tormented by the evil he saw day after day.

Now: Being grieved by the world’s evil is a mark of the righteous; being comfortable with it is the danger.

verseByVerse.quote: But false prophets also arose among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you, who will secretly bring in destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them, bringing upon themselves swift destruction. And many will follow their sensuality, and because of them the way of truth will be blasphemed. And in their greed they will exploit you with false words. Their condemnation from long ago is not idle, and their destruction is not asleep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 2 Peter 2 is a sustained warning against false teachers, who smuggle in heresies, deny the Master who bought them, and exploit believers out of greed (vv. 1–3). The angels, the flood and Sodom prove that God judges, and Noah and Lot that he knows how to rescue the godly (vv. 4–9). The teachers indulge the flesh, despise authority, and follow Balaam (vv. 10–16); promising freedom, they are slaves of corruption, and having escaped the world they are entangled again (vv. 17–22).

The setting. Much of this chapter closely parallels the letter of Jude. Which drew on which does not affect the meaning. The false teachers seem to have combined a denial of Christ’s return and future judgement (3:3–4) with moral licence: since there is no judgement coming, live as you please. They may have twisted Paul’s teaching on grace into permission to sin (3:15–16). After the true prophets carried along by the Spirit (1:21), Peter turns to the counterfeit.

False prophets also arose. In Israel’s history many claimed to speak for God but did not (Deuteronomy 13:1–5; 18:20–22; Jeremiah 23:9–40). Every true prophet had his shadow: Moses had Balaam, Jeremiah had Hananiah and a crowd crying peace, peace, when there was no peace (Jeremiah 6:14). Israel had them; the church will have them.

False teachers among you. Inside the church, not outside (Acts 20:29–30; Matthew 7:15), which is what makes them dangerous and hard to name. A persecutor is easy to recognise. A false teacher sits in the next pew, sings the same hymns, and uses the same vocabulary.

Secretly bring in destructive heresies. Pareisaxousin means to smuggle in alongside. Error rarely arrives as a replacement for the truth. It arrives as an addition, placed beside it, until one day the truth has been edged out of the room. Heresies, haireseis, originally meant choices: a man’s own preference set up against what was delivered.

Denying the Master who bought them. Denying, arnoumenoi, is disowning, by their teaching and their lives (Titus 1:16; Jude 4). The word is painful on Peter’s lips: it is the word used of his own three denials in the courtyard. He knows what it is to deny the Lord, and what it is to be brought back. These men deny him and have no tears. Master, despotēs, is the owner of slaves; bought, agorasanta, the slave-market word (1 Corinthians 6:20). The picture is of purchased slaves repudiating the man who paid for them, and their destruction, swift and sudden, is one they bring upon themselves.

Where Christians differ: does “the Master who bought them” prove Christ died for everyone, including those who perish? Arminians (Christians who hold that Christ died to make salvation possible for everyone, with each person’s free response deciding the outcome) and some others, including some Calvinists, cite this verse to argue that Christ paid for the sins of all, including false teachers who are finally lost. The Reformed view, often called definite or particular atonement, is that Christ died to secure the salvation of his people. Godly believers have long differed here, and the debate is about how wide Christ’s purpose was, not about whether his death is offered freely to all. This commentary’s view: Several points apply. The word is Master (despotēs), not Saviour or Redeemer; it pictures a slave-owner who has purchased slaves, and the false teachers deny his rightful ownership. Peter may be speaking of their own profession: they claimed to be bought by Christ and part of the church, and Peter describes them according to that profession, as one might speak of a church member. Or he may be echoing Deuteronomy 32:6, where Israel as a nation is said to have been bought by God, though many Israelites were not saved. The verse does not use the language of effective redemption from sin (as in 1 Peter 1:18–19). Scripture elsewhere teaches that Christ laid down his life for his sheep (John 10:11, 15), that his death actually secures the salvation of those for whom he died (Romans 8:32–34; Hebrews 10:14), and that the sheep are never lost (John 10:28). The best reading is that the false teachers professed to belong to the Master who purchased the church, and their denial exposed that profession as false.

Were these men ever saved? The chapter suggests not. They returned to their old ways like a dog to its vomit (v. 22), showing that their nature had never changed. They stood within the covenant community and enjoyed everything that came with it: the preaching, the fellowship, the table, the outward cleansing of a changed reputation. And they turned on the One who purchased the church. Peter is not writing a treatise on the extent of the atonement; he is using the language of ownership to make the ingratitude vivid. The lesson for us is not to puzzle over their secret state but to examine our own: do I merely belong to a church that Christ bought, or do I belong to Christ?

Many will follow their sensuality. Sensuality, aselgeia: shameless excess. And it is many who follow. False teaching is popular, because it usually offers what the flesh already wants; false living then looks for teaching that will excuse it. A teacher who promises comfort, success or freedom from rebuke is selling to an appetite already in the room, and Paul warned that people would gather teachers to suit their own passions (2 Timothy 4:3).

The way of truth will be blasphemed. The way of truth is Christianity (Acts 9:2), and its reputation suffers. Outsiders judge the way of truth by the people carrying its name (Romans 2:24), and this letter’s readers were already being slandered (1 Peter 2:12).

In their greed they will exploit you. Greed, pleonexia, is the craving for more. Exploit, emporeusontai, is a trading word, from which comes emporium: they will make merchandise of you. The congregation is the commodity. False words, plastois logois, are moulded words, from which comes plastic: words shaped to sell rather than to tell the truth.

Not idle, not asleep. From long ago God has pronounced judgement on such people (Jude 4). Not idle, ouk argei, is the same root as the ineffective Christian of 1:8; not asleep, ou nystazei, is the word used of the virgins who all grew drowsy (Matthew 25:5). Judgement has been on its way a long time, awake and moving.

How can I tell a false teacher from a true one who makes mistakes? Look at three things Peter names. First, what he does with Christ: does he deny the Master, his deity, his lordship, his atoning death, his return, or does he exalt him? Second, his life: is his teaching producing holiness or licence, in him and in those who follow him? Third, his motive: is he serving the flock or using it, for money, power or admiration? A sincere teacher may be wrong on secondary matters and still love Christ, live humbly and feed the sheep. Treat him as a brother. A teacher who denies Christ, excuses sin and enriches himself is what this chapter describes, however gifted.

What should I do if I suspect false teaching in my church? Do not gossip and do not panic. First test what is taught by Scripture, carefully and fairly (Acts 17:11; 1 John 4:1). If you are still concerned, speak privately to the person, or to your elders, who are charged with guarding the flock (Acts 20:28–31; Titus 1:9). Be specific about what was said and why it troubles you. If the elders themselves are teaching what denies the gospel and will not be corrected, you may need to leave for a faithful church, quietly and without bitterness. Pray for those being misled, and keep your own heart close to Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every theological disagreement is a destructive heresy. Peter is speaking of denying Christ, combined with immoral living and greed.

On a Tuesday. Test the teachers you listen to online and the books on your nightstand. Ask of each one: does this make Christ greater to me, and make me holier and more generous, or does it make me more comfortable with myself?
verseByVerse.note: Much of this chapter closely parallels the letter of Jude.

verseByVerse.quote: For if God did not spare angels when they sinned, but cast them into hell and committed them to chains of gloomy darkness to be kept until the judgment; if he did not spare the ancient world, but preserved Noah, a herald of righteousness, with seven others, when he brought a flood upon the world of the ungodly; if by turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes he condemned them to extinction, making them an example of what is going to happen to the ungodly;
verseByVerse.commentary:
If God did not spare angels. Peter argues from history in one long conditional (vv. 4–9): three judgements, and woven among them, two rescues. Did not spare, ouk epheisato, is the verb Paul uses of God not sparing his own Son (Romans 8:32): God did not spare the angels who sinned, because they deserved judgement. He did not spare his Son, who did not, so that he might spare us. The first case is the highest of creatures: if rank protected anybody it would have protected them, and it did not.

Cast them into hell. Hell here is Tartarus (tartarōsas), only here in the New Testament: the Greek term for the deepest place of confinement, which his readers would understand.

Chains of gloomy darkness. Chains, seirais; some manuscripts read sirois, pits. Gloomy darkness, zophos, is the darkness of the underworld. Kept, tēroumenous: held in custody for a trial that has not yet happened (Jude 6; Revelation 20:10). Not all demons are bound, since many are active (Ephesians 6:12); these particular angels are.

Which angels are these? Some take them as the angels who fell with Satan at the beginning. Others, following Jewish tradition, link them with the sons of God who sinned with human women before the flood (Genesis 6:1–4), as Jude 6–7 may also do; and the order here (angels, then the flood, then Sodom) follows Genesis, which suggests the Genesis 6 sin. Calvin and many Reformed writers read the sons of God in Genesis 6 as the godly line of Seth instead, and some take them as kings. Peter does not stop to settle it, and neither does this commentary; each view has been held by faithful readers. What is plain is that angels sinned, are now held for judgement, and will be judged. And the point stands either way: if God did not spare angels, he will not spare false teachers.

The ancient world. The flood (Genesis 6–8): the whole world except one family.

But preserved Noah. God did not merely judge; he preserved. Herald of righteousness, dikaiosynēs kēryx, is a preacher of righteousness. Genesis records no sermon, but Jewish tradition held that he warned his generation, and the ark itself was a proclamation: years of hammering in the sight of neighbours who thought him mad. Eight survived (1 Peter 3:20). Faithfulness is not measured by numbers.

The world of the ungodly. Ungodly, asebōn, means without regard for God. Noah’s world lived as though the true God did not matter. Jesus said they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day Noah entered the ark (Matthew 24:38).

Sodom and Gomorrah. The third example (Genesis 19). Their sins included sexual immorality and violence (Genesis 19:4–9; Jude 7), and also pride, excess and neglect of the poor (Ezekiel 16:49–50). The three build: the highest creatures, the whole world, the most notorious cities.

An example. Hypodeigma is a pattern set out as a warning, as the desolate country by the Dead Sea was in Jewish memory. Past judgements are previews of the final judgement (Luke 17:26–30).

Is it not harsh to talk about judgement like this? It would be harsh only if it were untrue, or if it were said without tears. God’s judgement is not a flaw in his love but the expression of his holiness and justice; a God who never judged evil would not be good. And look how Peter tells it: in every case judgement is accompanied by rescue, and it comes after long patience. God waited while Noah built; he would have spared Sodom for ten righteous people (Genesis 18:32). Speaking of judgement is a kindness when it moves people to flee to Christ, who bore it in their place. The cruel thing would be to stay silent.

For worship. The Lord shut Noah in with his own hand, and then the rain came. Outside the ark the waters were judgement; inside, the same waters lifted eight people above a drowned world and set them down on a washed earth. Jesus called his death a baptism he had to undergo (Luke 12:50), and the flood of judgement went over him; those who are in him are carried through it into a new creation, saved through the resurrection of Jesus Christ (1 Peter 3:21). He has never lost one soul that he shut in.
verseByVerse.note: “Hell” here is Tartarus, a Greek term for the deepest place of punishment.

verseByVerse.quote: and if he rescued righteous Lot, greatly distressed by the sensual conduct of the wicked (for as that righteous man lived among them day after day, he was tormenting his righteous soul over their lawless deeds that he saw and heard); then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials, and to keep the unrighteous under punishment until the day of judgment,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Righteous Lot. The surprise of the paragraph, because Genesis does not present Lot flatteringly. He chose the well-watered plain and pitched his tent toward Sodom (Genesis 13:10–13); he offered his daughters to the mob (19:8); he lingered when the angels told him to flee, and had to be dragged out by the hand (19:16); and the story of his family afterwards is squalid (19:30–38). Yet Peter calls him righteous three times in two verses. It is not sentimentality. Lot was righteous by faith, as Abraham was, and God rescued him (Genesis 19:15–16, 29). The word describes standing, not record: if Lot is righteous, it cannot mean impressive. Rescued, errysato, is the word in the Lord’s Prayer: deliver us from evil.

Greatly distressed. Kataponoumenon means worn down. The evidence Peter goes on is entirely inward. Lot did very little; what he did was suffer.

Tormenting his righteous soul. Genesis does not tell of Lot’s inner distress, though Lot did protest the men’s demands (Genesis 19:7). Peter reveals what Lot felt. Tormenting, ebasanizen, is a strong verb: the word for testing metal on a touchstone and for torment under interrogation. And day after day names the form it took: not one crisis but daily attrition, a man who had chosen to live there and could not stop being grieved by it. What he saw and heard got into him. Believers today should likewise be grieved, not entertained, by the wickedness around them.

A comfort for the compromised. For a believer living in the consequences of poor choices: if the mark of a righteous man in Sodom is that the place still distresses him, then the reader who feels worn down by the world around him has evidence rather than condemnation. The people who are comfortable are the ones in danger. And God rescued Lot even though he lingered: the angels seized him by the hand, the LORD being merciful to him (Genesis 19:16).

The Lord knows how to rescue. The conclusion of the long sentence (vv. 4–9). Knows how, oiden: the readers do not have to work out the mechanism. He found a boat for one and a road out of the city for the other. He knows how.

Rescued from the present evil age. Lot’s rescue is a small picture of a greater one. Angels went into Sodom to bring one man out; the Son of God came into this world itself, and did not merely take us by the hand but gave himself for our sins to deliver us from the present evil age (Galatians 1:4). And the verdict righteous, spoken over a man with Lot’s record, has only one explanation: God justifies the ungodly for the sake of another, the righteous one who suffered for the unrighteous (Romans 4:5; 1 Peter 3:18). God pronounces a guilty man righteous because the record of Christ is counted as his. The Lord knows how to rescue, and at the cross he showed how.

To keep the unrighteous under punishment. Keep, tērein, is the custody word of verse 4. Rescuing and keeping are one skill. Under punishment, kolazomenous, is a present participle: being punished. The wicked who have died are already experiencing punishment, held for the final judgement (Luke 16:23–24). Some translations take the participle as looking ahead, to be punished at the judgement, but the present tense most naturally means punishment already under way. On that reading the wicked dead are conscious, and in custody, not purification, until the judgement.

What if I live, like Lot, somewhere I chose badly? First, take comfort: God did not abandon Lot, and he will not abandon you. Second, take warning: Lot lost much in Sodom: his possessions, his sons-in-law, his wife, and his daughters’ moral compass, and you can lose a great deal by staying where you are drawn into sin. Ask honestly whether your work, neighbourhood, friendships or entertainment are wearing down your love for God or merely wearing you down with grief. If the first, seek a way out, as God may be providing one. If the second, stay faithful, keep praying, and let your grief become prayer for the people around you.

How can I be grieved by the world without becoming bitter or self-righteous? Remember that Lot’s grief came from love of righteousness, not contempt for people. Grieve over sin as one who has been forgiven much, not as one who is better. Pray for those whose deeds trouble you, that God would turn them from their ways. Speak truth gently when you can. And turn your distress toward God, not toward endless complaining about the culture; Lot’s torment was in his soul before the Lord. A heart grieved by sin and full of mercy for sinners looks like Christ, who wept over Jerusalem.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers will always be rescued from suffering in this life. It means God will finally rescue them, through death if necessary, and will never abandon them.
verseByVerse.note: Genesis does not tell of Lot’s inner distress, though Lot did call the men’s intent wicked (Gen 19:7); Peter draws out the inner side of it.
