verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–22 — The Portrait, and the Washed Sow
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter now describes the teachers themselves: reckless toward spiritual powers, driven by appetite, greedy like Balaam, preying on new believers with promises of freedom. Having known the way of righteousness and turned back, they are worse off than before.
verseByVerse.theology:
Washed, Not Changed

The false teachers promise freedom while slaves of corruption. The washed sow returns to the mire because her nature was never changed.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Like Balaam, they loved gain and preyed on unsteady new believers.

Now: The question is not whether you have been washed, but whether you have been changed.

verseByVerse.quote: and especially those who indulge in the lust of defiling passion and despise authority. Bold and willful, they do not tremble as they blaspheme the glorious ones, whereas angels, though greater in might and power, do not pronounce a blasphemous judgment against them before the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Defiling passion. Peter turns to the men themselves. Indulge, poreuomenous, is literally walk after: their desires lead and they follow. Defiling passion is polluting lust. The first mark is appetite.

And despise authority. Authority, kyriotēs, is lordship (on whose, see below). These men will not be told anything by anybody. And the two marks belong together: a man who wants to follow his appetites must first get rid of anyone who has the right to say no.

Bold and willful. Bold, tolmētai, is reckless. Willful, authadeis, is self-pleasing (Titus 1:7). Together they describe a confidence with no external check on it, which is exactly what makes a false teacher persuasive. Uncertain people are drawn to certainty, and these men never doubt themselves.

The glorious ones. Doxas, glories, are angelic beings, probably fallen angels or demons. The false teachers speak contemptuously of evil spirits, as men who have never considered that the unseen world might be real.

Whereas angels. Even holy angels, who know what these powers are and are far stronger, do not insult evil spirits but leave judgement to God. Jude 9 gives the example of the archangel Michael, in a story not told in the Old Testament but known from Jewish tradition, who, disputing with the devil over Moses’ body, did not rebuke him himself but said, “The Lord rebuke you.” Ignorance is producing the confidence.

The lordship they despise. The lordship these men wave away is most naturally the Lord’s own. They have already been described as denying the Master who bought them (v. 1), and in the parallel passage Jude says the same men reject authority (Jude 8). The one whose lordship they despise is the one before whom an unclean spirit cried out in the synagogue at Capernaum, I know who you are, the Holy One of God, and was silenced with a word (Mark 1:24–25). Michael would not pronounce judgement on the devil because judgement belongs to the Lord, and the Father has given all judgement to the Son (John 5:22). The men who joke about the powers are joking in front of their Judge.

How should a Christian deal with the devil, then? Firmly, humbly, and in Christ’s name, not our own. Resist him, firm in your faith (1 Peter 5:8–9; James 4:7). Put on the armour of God, which is truth, righteousness, the gospel, faith, salvation and the word (Ephesians 6:10–18). Pray. Flee temptation. You do not need to shout at demons, mock them, or seek them out; Michael simply appealed to the Lord. Nor do you need to fear them: greater is he who is in you (1 John 4:4). The posture is quiet confidence in Christ’s victory, not bravado and not terror.

What about authority I genuinely disagree with? Despising authority is not the same as disagreeing with it. You may question a decision, appeal respectfully, or, where an authority commands sin, obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). Where authority is abused, especially in cases of abuse of the vulnerable, it must be exposed and the victims protected; that is not rebellion but righteousness. What Peter condemns is the settled heart that refuses to be under anyone, God included, so that it can do as it pleases.

verseByVerse.quote: But these, like irrational animals, creatures of instinct, born to be caught and destroyed, blaspheming about matters of which they are ignorant, will also be destroyed in their destruction, suffering wrong as the wage for their wrongdoing. They count it pleasure to revel in the daytime. They are blots and blemishes, reveling in their deceptions, while they feast with you. They have eyes full of adultery, insatiable for sin. They entice unsteady souls. They have hearts trained in greed. Accursed children!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like irrational animals. Irrational, aloga, is the word logos negated: without reason. The comparison is diagnostic: they have exchanged reason for instinct, which is why arguing with them achieves nothing. Believers were made partakers of the divine nature; these men have sunk to the merely natural.

Born to be caught and destroyed. Like wild animals that end in hunters’ traps, men who live by appetite follow their nose to the bait and never see the snare. They speak loudest about what they understand least, and they will perish in their perishing: the ruin they bring on others is the ruin they receive.

Suffering wrong as the wage. A wordplay: being wronged as the wage of wrong. They wanted wages; they will get them (compare Balaam, v. 15).

To revel in the daytime. Revel, tryphē, is luxurious indulgence. Even in a Greek city serious drinking belonged to the night (1 Thessalonians 5:7); these people indulge in broad daylight. Shame has gone.

Blots and blemishes. Blots and blemishes reverse the gospel. Believers were ransomed with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Peter 1:19), and in 3:14 Peter will urge them to be found without spot or blemish. The spotless Lamb died to have a spotless people (Ephesians 5:25–27), and here are blemished men sitting at the very meals where the church remembered the unblemished Lamb, parodying everything his death was meant to produce.

While they feast with you. Deceptions, apatais; some manuscripts read agapais, love feasts, as in Jude 12. The false teachers took part in the church’s fellowship meals, turning them into self-indulgence.

Eyes full of adultery. Literally eyes full of an adulteress: men who cannot look at a woman without sizing her up as a possible conquest (Matthew 5:28). And insatiable, akatapaustous, never resting. That is the cruelty of every lust: it promises rest and delivers restlessness.

They entice unsteady souls. Entice, deleazontes, is to bait (James 1:14). Unsteady, astēriktous, is the opposite of the established believers of 1:12.

Hearts trained in greed. Trained, gegymnasmenēn, is the athlete’s word, the root of gymnasium. Not a lapse but a discipline, the word used of mature believers’ trained discernment (Hebrews 5:14). Everyone is in training for something.

Accursed children! Literally children of a curse: people under God’s curse. Peter’s exclamation is not a loss of temper but a cry of horror at what these men have become, and at where they are taking others.

Why is the Bible’s language about these men so harsh? Because the stakes are so high. These men are leading souls to destruction while feasting at the Lord’s Table. A shepherd who finds wolves among the flock does not describe them gently (Acts 20:29). Jesus spoke the same way of the scribes and Pharisees who shut the kingdom in people’s faces (Matthew 23). The harshness is love for the sheep. But note that it is aimed at those who teach and exploit, not at ordinary strugglers; to the weak and the wandering Scripture speaks with great tenderness (Matthew 12:20).

I struggle with lustful eyes. Am I like these men? There is a world of difference between a believer who fights lust and hates it, and a man whose eyes are full of it, who is insatiable, trains himself in it and teaches others to indulge. The first is a wounded soldier; the second is a deserter who has gone over to the enemy. A believer can both love a sin and hate it at once, and that inner war is itself the Spirit’s work in you (Romans 7:15–25; Galatians 5:17). If you are fighting, keep fighting: make a covenant with your eyes (Job 31:1), cut off what feeds it, bring it into the light with a trusted believer, and run to Christ each time you fall. The very fact that you grieve shows that you are not what this verse describes.

On a Tuesday. Ask what your habits are training you in: what you watch, scroll, spend on and daydream about. Not by willpower alone: the Spirit who made you a partaker of the divine nature trains you through the word, prayer and the company of believers, so replace one habit of the flesh with one habit of grace. You will not do it perfectly. Christ’s clean eyes and pure heart were his perfect obedience in your place, and they are counted as yours; so when you fail, begin again.

For worship. Every line of this portrait has its opposite in him. His eyes were full of compassion and never of lust; he did not bait the unsteady but gathered them, and carried the lambs in his arms. And children of a curse are exactly the people he came for. He bore the curse himself, so that the accursed might be called children of God and sit at his table, washed, filled and welcome.

verseByVerse.quote: Forsaking the right way, they have gone astray. They have followed the way of Balaam, the son of Beor, who loved gain from wrongdoing, but was rebuked for his own transgression; a speechless donkey spoke with human voice and restrained the prophet's madness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Forsaking the right way. Gone astray, eplanēthēsan, gives us planet, a wandering star. They knew the road, and they left it.

The way of Balaam. Most manuscripts, followed by the KJV, call his father Bosor, a variant form of the name; a few early ones read Beor, as in Numbers. Balaam is the exact case: a soothsayer to whom God really spoke (Joshua 13:22; Numbers 22:9–12), and who put that gift on the market. Balak of Moab offers money to have Israel cursed; Balaam wants the fee, but every time he opens his mouth, blessing comes out (Numbers 22–24). He later advises Balak how to lead Israel into sexual immorality and idolatry at Peor (Numbers 25:1–3; 31:16; Revelation 2:14), which is what he is remembered for (Jude 11).

Who loved gain from wrongdoing. Literally loved the wages of unrighteousness, echoing verse 13. It identifies the false teachers precisely: not men who set out to destroy the church but men who discovered that religion pays and adjusted their message to keep it paying. The problem was not that he was paid, but what he loved.

A speechless donkey. The reversal is the point: the prophet behaves like an animal, so an animal does the prophet’s job (Numbers 22:21–35). Madness, paraphronia, is being out of one’s mind. Balaam was not deceived; he had heard from God repeatedly and went anyway. The man who knows exactly what God has said and calculates that the money is worth it has lost his reason, whatever his gifts.

A star out of Jacob. The most remarkable thing Balaam ever said, he said against his will. Hired to curse, he was made to see far ahead: I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near: a star shall come out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel (Numbers 24:17). The man who loved wages was made to announce the King whose sceptre no money could buy. God can put the truth about his Son even into a mercenary’s mouth, but Balaam saw the star from far off and died among the enemies of the people it would rise over (Numbers 31:8). To see Christ and not love him is the deepest madness of all.

The mercy in the road. The angel stood in the road with a drawn sword, and the donkey turned aside three times and saved his life (Numbers 22:33). God often puts such obstacles in our way: a closed door, a rebuke, an illness, a word from an unexpected mouth. The question is whether we beat the donkey or listen to it.

How do I know whether I love money too much? Ask a few honest questions. Would I compromise truth or conscience to keep or gain it? Do I give generously and gladly, or grudgingly? Does the thought of losing it fill me with fear? Does it shape my decisions more than God’s word does? Do I resent others who have more? Love of money is a root of all kinds of evils (1 Timothy 6:10), and it hides well, especially in religious people. The cure is not only to hold it loosely but to love something better: to find Christ so satisfying that money returns to its proper place as a tool and not a god.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all who are paid for ministry are like Balaam. Workers deserve wages (1 Timothy 5:18). The sin is loving money and compromising truth for it.

On a Tuesday. A bank statement can be read as a spiritual document: what does yours say you love?
verseByVerse.note: Balaam was hired to curse Israel for money, and his donkey spoke to rebuke him.

verseByVerse.quote: These are waterless springs and mists driven by a storm. For them the gloom of utter darkness has been reserved. For, speaking loud boasts of folly, they entice by sensual passions of the flesh those who are barely escaping from those who live in error. They promise them freedom, but they themselves are slaves of corruption. For whatever overcomes a person, to that he is enslaved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Waterless springs. Promise without delivery: in that country a dry spring was danger. God had complained through Jeremiah that his people had forsaken him, the fountain of living waters, and dug broken cisterns that can hold no water (Jeremiah 2:13). False teachers are such cisterns.

Mists driven by a storm. Clouds raise the farmer’s hope and pass over without rain (Jude 12). These men are weather that does not break.

The gloom of utter darkness. The destiny of the false teachers is outer darkness (Matthew 8:12; 22:13; Jude 13). Reserved, tetērētai, is the custody word of verses 4 and 9. There is a grim fitness: men who promised light are held in the dark.

Loud boasts of folly. Loud boasts, hyperonka, are swelling, bombastic words; folly, mataiotēs, is emptiness (Romans 8:20). Empty as a drum, delivered confidently. And the bait is not intellectual; it is appetite.

Barely escaping. Oligōs apopheugontas is only a little escaping: new converts who have just left paganism. (The KJV’s clean escaped follows later manuscripts with a word meaning truly.) New converts, having just broken with a way of life at real cost, are told they need not have bothered.

They promise them freedom. Probably a twisted version of Christian freedom, claiming that grace means freedom from moral rules (Galatians 5:13; 1 Peter 2:16; Romans 6:1–2). It is the oldest lie in the world, the serpent’s promise in the garden: throw off God’s word and your eyes will be opened.

Slaves of corruption. Corruption is the moral decay of 1:4. Peter called himself a slave of Christ in 1:1, and these men, who promise freedom, are slaves of rot.

Whatever overcomes a person. Overcomes, hēttētai, is a battlefield word: the conquered become slaves. whatever masters you is your master (Romans 6:16). The man who throws off restraint has changed owners, and taken a worse one. Jesus said it first, and gave the only way out: everyone who practises sin is a slave to sin, and if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed (John 8:34–36). The Son gives freedom by breaking the old master’s hold at the cost of his own life, and taking his freed people under a yoke that is easy (Matthew 11:29–30).

What does real Christian freedom look like? It is freedom from the guilt of sin, because Christ has paid for it; freedom from the power of sin, because we are united to him; freedom from the law as a way of earning acceptance; and freedom from fear of death and judgement. But it is freedom for something: to love God and serve others (Galatians 5:13). A train is free on its rails and helpless off them; a fish is free in water and dies on the bank. We are free when we live as we were made to live, under the gentle rule of Christ, whose yoke is easy.

I have just come to faith and feel shaky. How do I avoid being lured? Stay close to the flock and to faithful shepherds; predators pick off the sheep that wander alone. Get into a Bible-teaching church and attend faithfully. Read Scripture daily, starting with a Gospel. Find an older believer to meet with and ask questions. Be wary of anyone who tells you that the sins you have left were not really so bad, or that grace means you need not change. And when temptation comes dressed as freedom, ask where it leads; the end of the road is what tells you the truth about it.

verseByVerse.quote: For if, after they have escaped the defilements of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and overcome, the last state has become worse for them than the first. For it would have been better for them never to have known the way of righteousness than after knowing it to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them. What the true proverb says has happened to them: "The dog returns to its own vomit, and the sow, after washing herself, returns to wallow in the mire."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After they have escaped. Among the most sobering verses in the New Testament. They are the false teachers, and perhaps those they led astray. Escaped is the word of 1:4. These men had genuinely got out of their former life, at the level anyone could see, and had known the gospel, perhaps professed it.

Again entangled and overcome. Entangled, emplakentes, is woven in, like a fish in a net. Overcome is the word of verse 19: conquered again by the master they once escaped.

The last state worse than the first. Peter is echoing his Master’s words about a house swept clean and reoccupied by seven worse spirits, so that the last state is worse than the first (Matthew 12:45; Luke 11:26). Having known the truth and rejected it, they are more guilty and more hardened than before.

Better never to have known. The plain sense should not be blunted. Greater knowledge brings greater responsibility (Luke 12:47–48; Hebrews 6:4–6; 10:26–29): a man who has seen and turned away is in a worse position than one who never saw. The holy commandment is the Christian faith and way of life, delivered by the apostles (Jude 3). It was handed to them, and they put it down.

The true proverb. How does this stand with the perseverance of the saints, the teaching that those God truly saves he keeps to the end? Peter himself supplies the answer, and it is the reason the proverb is there.

The dog returns to its own vomit. From Proverbs 26:11. Dogs were despised scavengers. The dog gets rid of what was making it sick, and then goes back to it, because it is still a dog.

The sow, after washing herself. A popular proverb. The sow has been washed, genuinely and visibly; what she has not been given is a different nature. She returns to the mud because she is still a pig, and washing a pig does not make it a sheep. That is Peter’s verdict: not that they lost salvation, but that they were cleaned rather than changed, the heart never renewed, which is exactly what 1 John 2:19 says of those who went out from us because they were not of us.

Clean, but not every one of you. Peter had heard this distinction drawn by the Lord himself, the night his own feet were washed. The one who has bathed, Jesus said, is completely clean; and you are clean, but not every one of you, for he knew who was to betray him (John 13:10–11). Judas, it seems, had his feet washed by the hands of Christ, and went out into the night. Outward washing, even at Jesus’ hands, is not belonging to him. The cleansing that changes a nature is the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, poured out through Jesus Christ our Saviour (Titus 3:5–6).

Where Christians differ: does this passage show that true believers can lose salvation? Arminian Christians, who hold that a true believer may finally turn away and be lost, read the passage so, pointing to escaped and to knowledge of our Lord and Saviour. Many of them are earnest, godly believers, and the warning they stress is real. This commentary’s view: The proverbs answer the question. The dog and the sow returned to filth because their nature had never been changed; they were washed outwardly but remained dogs and pigs. These people had external knowledge of Christ and outward moral reform, but never received a new nature (1:4). True believers, made partakers of the divine nature, are kept by God’s power (1 Peter 1:5) and will never finally fall (1:10). Those who return permanently to their former life show they were never truly regenerated (1 John 2:19).

How can someone know so much and never be truly saved? Because knowing about Christ is not the same as being united to him. Judas walked with Jesus for about three years, heard every sermon and saw every miracle. People can be moved by the gospel, reform their habits, join a church, even teach, and yet never have been born again (Matthew 7:21–23; 13:20–21). The difference is not how much they knew but whether the Spirit gave them a new heart. That is why the test is not how impressive a conversion looked, but what a person keeps returning to over time.

I have gone back to an old sin. Am I the dog returning to its vomit? Not if you hate it and want to be free. The dog returns to its vomit gladly, because it is what a dog loves. A child of God may fall back into sin, sometimes badly and repeatedly, but he is miserable there, he confesses it, and he longs to be clean (Psalm 51; 1 John 1:9). Peter himself denied Christ three times and was restored. If you are grieved, go to Christ today. He has not changed his mind about you, and the new nature in you is the very thing that makes the mud unbearable.

On a Tuesday. This passage is meant not to make believers anxious but honest. Its question is not whether you have been washed but whether you have been changed, and the evidence is what you find yourself returning to when you are tired, alone and unwatched. Thank God for every sign that you now love what you once hated; and where the old pull remains, bring it to him today.

For worship. The Lord Jesus does not wash pigs and leave them pigs. He gives a new heart and puts a new spirit within, so that what we once loved becomes our grief, and what we once despised becomes our joy. The dog returns to its vomit; the sheep returns to its Shepherd, because his voice is the one it now loves, and no one will snatch it out of his hand.

2.theology: The chapter’s controlling question is apostasy: can a person who has genuinely known Christ fall finally away? The Reformed answer is that those truly born again will persevere (John 10:28–29; Romans 8:38–39). But the visible church contains people who share its privileges without its life, and it is these who can have the knowledge described in verse 20 and still return to their former state. The dog and the sow mark the boundary: the animal’s nature is unchanged. Outward reform without a new heart ends in worse corruption. This is not a loophole in the doctrine of perseverance; it is the setting in which the doctrine is honestly held.
2.examples: The Balaam portrait (vv. 15–16) gives a congregation a plain test. What does this teacher gain from what he teaches? Balaam’s gift was real, but it became a commodity. The test of a ministry is not whether the gifts are real but whether the teacher loves the Lord more than the wages.

3.title: The Day That Is Coming
3.overview:
The last chapter is the letter’s goal. The false teachers attack the hope of Christ’s return, and with it the reason for holy living.

Peter answers in three steps. The world has not always continued as it was: God’s word created it and judged it by the flood, and the same word holds it now for judgment. God is not slow, but patient, giving time for repentance. And the day will come suddenly and lay everything bare. So the question is not “When?” but “What sort of people ought you to be?”
3.text: <sup>1</sup>This is now the second letter that I am writing to you, beloved. In both of them I am stirring up your sincere mind by way of reminder,<sup>2</sup>that you should remember the predictions of the holy prophets and the commandment of the Lord and Savior through your apostles,<sup>3</sup>knowing this first of all, that scoffers will come in the last days with scoffing, following their own sinful desires.<sup>4</sup>They will say, "Where is the promise of his coming? For ever since the fathers fell asleep, all things are continuing as they were from the beginning of creation."<sup>5</sup>For they deliberately overlook this fact, that the heavens existed long ago, and the earth was formed out of water and through water by the word of God,<sup>6</sup>and that by means of these the world that then existed was deluged with water and perished.<sup>7</sup>But by the same word the heavens and earth that now exist are stored up for fire, being kept until the day of judgment and destruction of the ungodly.<sup>8</sup>But do not overlook this one fact, beloved, that with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day.<sup>9</sup>The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.<sup>10</sup>But the day of the Lord will come like a thief, and then the heavens will pass away with a roar, and the heavenly bodies will be burned up and dissolved, and the earth and the works that are done on it will be exposed.<sup>11</sup>Since all these things are thus to be dissolved, what sort of people ought you to be in lives of holiness and godliness,<sup>12</sup>waiting for and hastening the coming of the day of God, because of which the heavens will be set on fire and dissolved, and the heavenly bodies will melt as they burn!<sup>13</sup>But according to his promise we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells.<sup>14</sup>Therefore, beloved, since you are waiting for these, be diligent to be found by him without spot or blemish, and at peace.<sup>15</sup>And count the patience of our Lord as salvation, just as our beloved brother Paul also wrote to you according to the wisdom given him,<sup>16</sup>as he does in all his letters when he speaks in them of these matters. There are some things in them that are hard to understand, which the ignorant and unstable twist to their own destruction, as they do the other Scriptures.<sup>17</sup>You therefore, beloved, knowing this beforehand, take care that you are not carried away with the error of lawless people and lose your own stability.<sup>18</sup>But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Scoffers and the Day
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter reminds his readers of the prophets and the apostles, and warns that scoffers will mock the promise of Christ’s coming. He answers them from creation and the flood, from God’s relation to time, and from his patience, and warns that the day will still come like a thief.
verseByVerse.theology:
Not Slowness but Patience

The world has not always continued as it was: God’s word made it and judged it by the flood. The Lord is not slow but patient, and the day will come like a thief.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Scoffers pointed to the death of the first generation as proof that nothing was coming.

Now: The delay is mercy; the right response is repentance, not argument about the timetable.

verseByVerse.quote: This is now the second letter that I am writing to you, beloved. In both of them I am stirring up your sincere mind by way of reminder, that you should remember the predictions of the holy prophets and the commandment of the Lord and Savior through your apostles,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 2 Peter 3 answers the denial of Christ’s return. Scoffers say nothing has changed since creation (vv. 1–4); but God made the world by his word, judged it by water, and keeps it for fire (vv. 5–7). His delay is patience, not wishing any to perish (vv. 8–9). The day will come like a thief (v. 10), so live holy lives, waiting for new heavens and a new earth where righteousness dwells (vv. 11–16), and grow in the grace and knowledge of Christ (vv. 17–18).

The second letter. The earlier letter is most likely 1 Peter. Beloved, agapētoi, comes four times in this chapter (vv. 1, 8, 14, 17), a warm contrast with the harsh words about false teachers.

Stirring up your sincere mind. Stirring up, diegeirō, is the waking verb again from 1:13: his readers do not need new material; they need rousing. Sincere, eilikrinē, means pure, unmixed. Peter credits them with genuineness even as he warns them: a sound mind is not a mind beyond the reach of drowsiness.

The predictions of the holy prophets. The Old Testament prophets foretold the Day of the Lord, judgement and new creation (Isaiah 65:17; 66:22; Joel 2; Daniel 7; 12). The defence against what follows is memory.

Through your apostles. The commandment is the apostolic teaching, including Christ’s promise to return, and they are your apostles: not a distant institution but the men who actually brought them the gospel. Prophets and apostles stand side by side, equal in weight (compare v. 16; Ephesians 2:20), and they meet in one Person. The risen Lord opened his disciples’ minds to see that everything written about him in the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled (Luke 24:44–45); the prophets foretold him, the apostles were sent by him, and the commandment is his own.

Why does it matter that the prophets and apostles are put together? Because it means the whole Bible speaks with one voice and one authority. The Old Testament is not a lesser, outdated book, and the New Testament is not merely the church’s opinion about Jesus. Both are God’s word. So when you read about the day of the Lord in Joel or Zephaniah and then in Peter, you are hearing one story told by one Author, promised in the one and explained in the other. Read them together, and let each shed light on the other.

On a Tuesday. Pick one promise of Christ’s return and read it each morning this week: Acts 1:11, John 14:3, or Isaiah 65:17–25. And thank God for whoever first brought you the apostles’ message.
verseByVerse.note: The earlier letter is most likely 1 Peter.

verseByVerse.quote: knowing this first of all, that scoffers will come in the last days with scoffing, following their own sinful desires. They will say, "Where is the promise of his coming? For ever since the fathers fell asleep, all things are continuing as they were from the beginning of creation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Knowing this first of all. As in 1:20. Before you hear the scoffers, know that they were foretold.

Scoffers will come in the last days. Scoffers with scoffing, empaiktai en empaigmonē, a Hebrew-style emphasis. Every scoffer is, without meaning to be, a fulfilled prophecy. The last days are the whole period since Christ’s first coming (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2; Jude 18).

Following their own sinful desires. Peter names the motive before the argument. Their doctrine has a cause, and the cause is not intellectual: if there is no coming judgement, there is no reason to restrain oneself. Peter is describing these particular mockers; he is not saying that every honest doubter is hiding a sin.

They will say, Where is the promise of his coming? Then the taunt itself. “Promise of his coming” (hē epangelia tēs parousias autou) is Jesus’ promise to return (John 14:3; Acts 1:11). The mocking question echoes Old Testament scoffers, who asked the psalmist all the day long where his God was (Psalm 42:3), and who asked, where is the God of justice? (Malachi 2:17).

The promise was his own. The scoffers are mocking not a church doctrine but the word of Jesus: I will come again and will take you to myself (John 14:3). They are not the first to mock his promises. At the cross the chief priests jeered, he saved others; he cannot save himself (Matthew 27:42), and afterwards called him the impostor who had said he would rise after three days (Matthew 27:63). On the third day the tomb was empty. The promise mocked once was kept once, and that is the pledge of the next: God has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead (Acts 17:31).

Ever since the fathers fell asleep. The fathers are probably the first generation of Christians, who had died, or perhaps the Old Testament patriarchs. Fell asleep, ekoimēthēsan, a common Christian word for dying (1 Thessalonians 4:13–15), already carries the hope of waking. (It describes the body; the soul is with Christ, Philippians 1:23.) The argument has two parts. The first: the first generation had died and nothing had happened, a real problem in a church burying its founders. Many scholars take this line as a sign that the letter was written after the apostles’ generation had died, and so after Peter. But by the mid-60s many first believers had died, Stephen and James among them, and if the fathers are the patriarchs the phrase says nothing about date at all.

All things are continuing as they were. The second part is the argument from uniformity: the world is a closed system; God does not intervene; there will be no judgement. It sounds very modern. Peter does not dispute that the sun rises every morning; he disputes the conclusion, by pointing to two occasions when things did not continue as they were.

Is it wrong to wonder why Christ has not yet come? No. Honest questions are not scoffing. The souls under the altar cry, how long? (Revelation 6:10), and the psalms are full of it. What Peter condemns is mocking unbelief that uses the delay as an excuse to live as one pleases. The difference lies in the heart: the scoffer asks where is he? hoping the answer is nowhere; the believer asks where is he? because he longs to see him. If your question comes from longing, it is a kind of prayer: come, Lord Jesus.

How should I answer someone who says the world just runs by natural laws? Agree that the world is wonderfully regular, and then ask why. The regularity of nature is not an argument against God but evidence of his faithful upholding of all things by the word of his power (Hebrews 1:3; Genesis 8:22). Laws describe how things normally go; they do not forbid the Lawgiver from acting. And history itself is not a closed loop: it had a beginning, it has seen a resurrection, and Scripture says it is moving toward an end. Be gentle, and point the conversation to Jesus’ resurrection, which is the decisive interruption.

On a Tuesday. Is there any area of your life where you live as though he were not coming, because you would rather he did not see it yet? Bring that into the light today; he who is coming forgives all who confess (1 John 1:9).

verseByVerse.quote: For they deliberately overlook this fact, that the heavens existed long ago, and the earth was formed out of water and through water by the word of God, and that by means of these the world that then existed was deluged with water and perished. But by the same word the heavens and earth that now exist are stored up for fire, being kept until the day of judgment and destruction of the ungodly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They deliberately overlook this fact. Lanthanei thelontas: this escapes their notice because they want it to. Their ignorance is chosen (Romans 1:18–21).

By the word of God. The first fact they ignore: God made the world by his word (Genesis 1; Hebrews 11:3), and in Genesis 1 the earth emerged from the waters (1:2, 6–10). The claim that all things continue as they were from the beginning of creation collapses at the word creation.

Deluged with water and perished. The second fact they ignore: the flood. Deluged, kataklystheis, gives us cataclysm. The water the world was formed through later destroyed it. Two strokes complete the argument: twice the world’s state was changed by the word of God, in Scriptures the scoffers claim to respect.

Was the flood worldwide? Genesis describes a flood that covered all the high mountains under the whole heaven (Genesis 7:19), and Peter sets it beside the coming judgement of the whole earth by fire (2 Peter 3:6–7). Most Christians have read it as worldwide, while some godly scholars hold that it covered the whole inhabited region rather than the whole earth. On either reading it was a real judgement, and Noah’s rescue a real salvation.

By the same word. One word made it, flooded it, and holds it now. The present stability is not inertia; it is sustained by the same voice that could end it. Stored up, tethēsaurismenoi, is treasured up. The next judgement will be by fire, not water: God promised Noah never again to destroy the earth by a flood (Genesis 9:11), and the prophets speak of fire (Isaiah 66:15–16; Malachi 4:1; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–8).

The Word who holds it. The New Testament puts a face on the same word. All things were made through the eternal Word (John 1:3), and the Son upholds the universe by the word of his power (Hebrews 1:3). The world is kept for judgement by the Lord who will be revealed from heaven in flaming fire (2 Thessalonians 1:7–8). And for the same reason the waiting world is kept for mercy: the one who holds back the fire is the Son who came the first time not to condemn the world but to save it (John 3:17).

Being kept until the day of judgment. Kept, tēroumenoi, is the custody word again, as of the angels in 2:4. The universe is not a machine running down but something held in reserve. Destruction, apōleia, is ruin: for the ungodly, eternal ruin.

What it does not mean. Destruction does not mean annihilation of the ungodly. Scripture describes their punishment as eternal and conscious (Matthew 25:46; Revelation 14:11; 20:10). The word means ruin, loss of all that makes existence good. Some evangelical Christians hold that the lost will finally cease to exist; this commentary respects them but holds the historic view, chiefly because Jesus sets eternal punishment beside eternal life in the same sentence (Matthew 25:46).

Should a Christian fear that the world will end in a nuclear war or climate disaster? We should care for God’s creation and work for peace, because we are stewards of what he made. But we need not live in terror that human beings will end the world before God’s time. The heavens and earth are kept by his word for his day. History will not end by accident or by our hand, but when and as he has appointed. That frees us both from despair and from the burden of thinking we must save the planet ourselves. Do your duty calmly, and trust the Keeper.

For worship. He spoke, and the dry land appeared; he spoke again, and the deep broke open; he speaks still, and the earth keeps its seasons. And for his people the coming fire holds no terror, because judgement has already broken over another: the Son bore in his own body the wrath that their sins had stored up. Blessed be the God who made the world by a word, and will make it new by the same.

verseByVerse.quote: But do not overlook this one fact, beloved, that with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not overlook this one fact. The verb of verse 5, turned round: the scoffers deliberately forget; believers must not.

One day is as a thousand years. The line echoes Psalm 90:4: a thousand years in your sight are but as yesterday when it is past. To a creature with seventy or eighty years, a delay of two millennia seems decisive; to the One who made time it is not a delay at all. The scoffers’ argument depends entirely on assuming God experiences duration the way they do.

Both halves are needed. The comparison runs both ways, which makes arithmetic useless. A thousand years as one day means the long wait is nothing to him. One day as a thousand years means no single day is trivial to him: he gives each day of your life the attention of a thousand years.

The Lord of the thousand years. Peter’s Lord is not a distant clock-keeper. The one for whom a thousand years are as a day is the Son who could say, before Abraham was, I am (John 8:58), and who then lived some thirty years of ordinary days in Nazareth before his hour came. Eternity entered time, so the delay is not the absence of someone who cannot feel the wait. And if any single day has carried the weight of a thousand years, it was the day he said, it is finished (John 19:30).

Where Christians differ: does this verse teach a thousand-year day or a millennial scheme? Some have used this verse to calculate the timing of Christ’s return, such as six thousand years of history followed by a thousand-year millennium. This commentary’s view: The verse is not a formula for calculation; it teaches that God’s perspective on time differs from ours. It warns against date-setting, not encourages it (Matthew 24:36; Acts 1:7). It gives no support to elaborate millennial timetables. (Christians differ on the thousand years of Revelation 20 itself, whether it is a future earthly reign of Christ or his present reign from heaven; this verse does not decide that question.)

Does this mean that the days of creation were long ages? This verse does not say so. Peter is speaking of how God relates to time, to explain the delay of Christ’s coming; the verse is not a conversion table, and reading it as one has produced a great deal of confusion. The days of Genesis 1 must be read from Genesis itself, and read there they are six ordinary days: each is numbered and closed with evening and morning, and the fourth commandment grounds our working week in God’s six days of making (Exodus 20:11). Whatever view a Christian takes of that question, this verse does not settle it, because it is not about creation at all. This commentary holds that God made all things in six ordinary days. Other faithful Christians read the days as long ages, as a literary framework for the week of creation, or as God’s workdays described by analogy with ours, often because they weigh the evidence for an old earth or the careful shape of the chapter; they deserve a patient hearing, and all agree that God made all things by his word.

Why would God make his people wait so long? Peter gives the main answer in the next verse: patience, so that more may repent. But consider too that waiting is how God grows faith. Abraham waited twenty-five years for Isaac; Israel waited centuries for the Messiah; Simeon waited, perhaps for many years, to hold the child. In the waiting, God tests and refines his people, teaches them to walk by faith and not sight, and gathers in his elect. The wait is long to us, but it is not empty. It is full of his purposes.

parallels.desc: a thousand years in your sight are but as yesterday

verseByVerse.quote: The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not slow to fulfill his promise. Slow, bradynei, is to loiter. The slowness exists only as some count it.

But is patient toward you. The heart of the chapter. Patient, makrothymei, is literally long of temper, slow to anger. Toward you: the readers, God’s beloved people (v. 1), the chosen (1 Peter 1:1). The delay is not indifference or forgetfulness but patience. The scoffers were treating the interval as evidence against God; Peter says it is evidence of his mercy, and that they are standing inside the very thing they are mocking.

Not wishing that any should perish. God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 18:23, 32; 33:11), and his patience gives time for repentance, metanoia, a change of mind and direction (Romans 2:4).

The patience of our Lord. Peter will tell them to count the patience of our Lord as salvation (v. 15), and the New Testament shows that patience with a human face. Paul, once a persecutor, wrote that he received mercy so that in him, the foremost of sinners, Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience as an example to those who would believe (1 Timothy 1:15–16). It is the patience of the Saviour himself, who wept over Jerusalem, prayed for those who crucified him, and reigns now while the last of his sheep are gathered in.

Where Christians differ: if God wishes all to repent, why are not all saved? Arminians read this verse as showing that God wills every individual to be saved and that human choice makes the difference; universalists as showing that all will eventually be saved. Reformed and Arminian Christians have long differed here, and both want to honour God’s mercy. This commentary’s view: The context helps: God is patient toward you, addressing believers, the beloved, the elect. The delay of Christ’s return is so that all of God’s people, including those not yet converted, may come to repentance before the end. When the last of the elect has been brought in, Christ will return. At the same time, Scripture teaches that God sincerely desires the repentance of all sinners in the sense that he delights in repentance and offers the gospel freely to all (Ezekiel 33:11; 1 Timothy 2:4), while he has also sovereignly chosen to save some and not all. These two truths, God’s revealed desire and his decreed purpose, are both taught, and must both be held. Universalism contradicts the next verse and the clear teaching of eternal judgement.

The use of the verse. What neither emphasis permits is the conclusion the scoffers wanted, that the delay means nothing is coming. If God is holding the door open, the response of anyone still outside it is not to argue about the mechanism but to walk through.

If God has chosen his elect, why should I evangelise? Because God has chosen the means as well as the end. The elect are brought to repentance through the gospel being preached (Romans 10:14–17), and God waits so that the gospel may reach them. Election is the great encouragement to evangelism, not its enemy: Paul was told to keep speaking in Corinth because the Lord had many people in that city (Acts 18:9–10). You do not know who the elect are, so offer Christ freely to everyone, sincerely, as God himself does. Every day of patience is a day for the gospel.

I have a loved one who has not repented. Is it too late? Not while they are alive, and not while the Lord is patient. This verse is a reason to keep praying and keep loving. God waited for you, perhaps for years. He knows how to bring the hardest heart to repentance, as he did with Saul of Tarsus. So pray specifically, live kindly before them, speak of Christ when doors open, and leave the timing with God. His patience is not reluctance to save; it is room being made for repentance.

verseByVerse.quote: But the day of the Lord will come like a thief, and then the heavens will pass away with a roar, and the heavenly bodies will be burned up and dissolved, and the earth and the works that are done on it will be exposed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like a thief. The day of the Lord is the Old Testament term for God’s great day of judgement and salvation (Joel 2:31; Amos 5:18–20; Zephaniah 1:14–18), now identified with Christ’s return. The thief image is the Lord’s own (Matthew 24:43; 1 Thessalonians 5:2). It conveys not stealth but unpredictability: this thief does not come quietly, for the heavens will roar. The scoffers asked where the promise was; the promise includes the fact that you will not see it coming.

With a roar. Pass away, pareleusontai, is the word Jesus used: heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away (Matthew 24:35). With a roar, rhoizēdon, imitates a rushing noise, like the crackle of a great fire.

Burned up and dissolved. The heavenly bodies, stoicheia, elements, are either the basic elements of the physical world, or the sun, moon and stars (Isaiah 34:4). Dissolved, lythēsetai, is the word for untying something. Either way the dissolution of the present order is total.

Will be exposed. The most important clause. Exposed, heurethēsetai, is will be found, laid bare: not mere destruction but disclosure. The fire is not chiefly an incinerator but a searchlight. Everything done on this earth will be brought into the open before God’s judgement (1 Corinthians 3:13; Hebrews 4:13), and the eyes that see it will be his: we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10), the one whose eyes are like a flame of fire (Revelation 1:14). Peter’s point against men living as they pleased is not only that the world will end but that it will be examined. That is hard news for a heart that lives for its reputation, because what other people think of us is exactly what the fire will not consult. And it is good news for anyone who has been wronged in secret and never vindicated: on that day the truth will come out.

Textual note. The manuscripts differ at the end of this verse. The oldest read will be found or exposed (heurethēsetai); later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read will be burned up (katakaēsetai); some read will not be found. The more difficult reading, will be found, is most likely original, meaning laid bare before God’s judgement.

Where Christians differ: is the day of the Lord a single event? Dispensationalists (who see God’s plan in distinct stages, with separate futures for Israel and the church) often separate a secret rapture of the church from a later visible return, and place a thousand-year earthly kingdom between Christ’s return and the final judgement and new creation. Other premillennial Christians, who reject a secret rapture, still see a sequence: Christ’s return, a thousand-year reign, then the final judgement and new creation. This commentary’s view: Peter places Christ’s coming, the day of the Lord, the judgement of the ungodly, and the dissolution of the present heavens and earth together in one great event, followed by the new heavens and new earth (vv. 7, 10, 12–13). This fits the amillennial understanding (that the thousand years of Revelation 20 describe Christ’s present reign, not a later earthly kingdom): one visible return of Christ, at which the dead are raised, all are judged, and creation is renewed. There is no secret rapture and no intervening earthly millennium. Many faithful Christians hold premillennial or dispensational views, and every one of them shares the hope this chapter teaches: Christ is coming, visibly and in glory, and his people must be ready. This commentary differs from them on the order of events, not on the hope.

If he comes like a thief, does that not mean a secret coming? No. The thief image describes the timing, not the manner. The same Lord who said he would come like a thief said that his coming would be like lightning flashing from east to west (Matthew 24:27), and that every eye will see him (Revelation 1:7). Here in Peter, the thief’s arrival is accompanied by the roar of the heavens. It will be sudden for everyone and secret to no one. That is why believers need not fear being left behind in a silent disappearance; we are called instead to be ready at any hour for a return that will fill the sky.

Will the earth then be annihilated, or renewed? Some Christians hold that the old creation will be destroyed and replaced, pointing to pass away and dissolved. But Peter compares it to the flood, which cleansed the world rather than abolishing it (v. 6), and says the earth will be exposed, laid bare to judgement. Paul says creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption (Romans 8:21). The more likely reading is that the present creation will be purged by fire and renewed, not abolished.

Should I try to work out when it will happen? No. Jesus said that no one knows the day or the hour (Matthew 24:36), and that it is not for us to know the times or seasons the Father has fixed (Acts 1:7). Every attempt to set dates has failed and brought the faith into ridicule. The signs Jesus gave (wars, false teachers, persecution, the gospel to the nations) mark the whole age, so that every generation should be ready. Scripture also names some things that come first: the gospel preached to all nations (Matthew 24:14), and a great falling away with the man of lawlessness revealed (2 Thessalonians 2:1–4). So his coming is near and always to be expected, yet not without named events before it, and never to be dated. The right response to a thief who comes at an unknown hour is not to calculate the hour but to keep the house ready at all hours.

On a Tuesday. If Christ came today, what would be exposed in your life? Christ has already borne what the fire would find, so this is not terror; but deal with the thing you would hurry to hide, and you will say more easily, come, Lord Jesus.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–18 — New Heavens, and the Last Command
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Since everything will be dissolved and laid bare, Peter asks what kind of people believers should be: holy and godly, waiting for new heavens and a new earth where righteousness is at home. Forewarned, they are to read Scripture humbly and grow in the grace and knowledge of Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Answer to Error Is Growth

Since everything will be laid bare, live in holiness and godliness while waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells. The last command is to grow in the grace and knowledge of Christ.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter called Paul a beloved brother and counted his letters among the Scriptures.

Now: A growing believer is far harder to uproot than one who is merely on guard.

verseByVerse.quote: Since all these things are thus to be dissolved, what sort of people ought you to be in lives of holiness and godliness, waiting for and hastening the coming of the day of God, because of which the heavens will be set on fire and dissolved, and the heavenly bodies will melt as they burn! But according to his promise we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All these things are thus to be dissolved. A present participle: as good as dissolving already. Everything you can see has a date stamped on it that you cannot read.

What sort of people ought you to be. Not speculation, not date-setting, not withdrawal: the question is about character. Holiness, hagiais anastrophais, is holy ways of life, and it is plural: in every area. Holiness is belonging to God and becoming like him: as he who called you is holy, Peter had written, be holy in all your conduct (1 Peter 1:15). Godliness is plural too: concrete acts. The teaching about the last things is for transformation, not speculation (1 John 3:2–3). If the house is to be pulled down, you do not spend your life polishing its brass; you invest in what will last.

Waiting for and hastening. Waiting, prosdokōntas, is looking for eagerly, as a family watches the road for a returning son. Hastening, speudontas, ordinarily means to speed something up. Since the delay is God’s patience, waiting for repentance, believers can, in some sense, hasten the day: by holy living, by prayer (your kingdom come, Matthew 6:10), and by evangelism, which brings in the elect whose conversion the Lord awaits (v. 9; Matthew 24:14). That is a dignity given to ordinary Christian obedience.

Will melt as they burn! The description is bleak, until verse 13 turns it round. Melt, tēketai, as in Isaiah 34:4 in the Greek, and Micah 1:4, where the mountains melt under the LORD like wax before the fire.

New heavens and a new earth. The point of the passage, and his promise (Isaiah 65:17; 66:22): the scoffers asked, where is the promise? Here it is. New, kainous, suggests new in quality, renewed: not merely a new universe in time, but a transformed one in kind (Revelation 21:1–5; Romans 8:19–21). The fire is not the end of the material world; what follows is a new earth, physical and renewed, with resurrected people in resurrected bodies living in a world set free.

In which righteousness dwells. Dwells, katoikei, is settles down, makes its permanent home. In the present world righteousness is a visitor often turned away at the door; in the new creation it will be at home. No more sin, injustice, evil or death (Revelation 21:4, 27). That clause answers chapter 2’s men who seemed to get away with it. And righteousness at home means the Righteous One at home among his people: behold, the dwelling place of God is with man (Revelation 21:3).

What will the new heavens and new earth actually be like? Scripture gives us glimpses rather than a map, but the glimpses are glorious. It will be a real, physical world, this creation renewed, as our risen bodies will be these bodies glorified (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). God will dwell with his people; there will be no more tears, death, mourning or pain (Revelation 21:3–4). There will be work without frustration, worship without weariness, fellowship without sin, and the glory of the nations brought in (Revelation 21:24–26). Above all, we will see his face (Revelation 22:4). Whatever is good in this world will be there, freed from the curse, and Christ will be its light.

If this world will be dissolved, does it matter what I do with it now? Yes, very much. The new creation is this creation renewed, not discarded, so faithful work done in the Lord is not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58). Caring for creation, doing justice, raising children, making things well, healing the sick: all of it honours the God who will renew the earth. What will not survive is sin, and whatever was done for self rather than for God (1 Corinthians 3:12–15). So hold this world loosely and serve it diligently: loosely, because it is passing; diligently, because it is his.

What it does not mean. Hastening does not mean we control God’s timetable or can force his hand. It means God uses his people’s prayers, holiness and witness in bringing about his purposes.

On a Tuesday. Pray your kingdom come, and mean it: the Spirit, God’s pledge of that new world, already lives in you. Then choose one concrete act of holiness today: an apology, an honest word, a gift, a conversation about Christ. Each is a brick in a house that will not burn.

For worship. The fire is not the end. Beyond the roar and the melting is the promise: new heavens and a new earth, where righteousness is at home, and where the Lord who was a stranger in his own world, and had no home of his own in it, will dwell with his people for ever. He will wipe away every tear with his own hand, and he does not lie.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, beloved, since you are waiting for these, be diligent to be found by him without spot or blemish, and at peace. And count the patience of our Lord as salvation, just as our beloved brother Paul also wrote to you according to the wisdom given him, as he does in all his letters when he speaks in them of these matters. There are some things in them that are hard to understand, which the ignorant and unstable twist to their own destruction, as they do the other Scriptures.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since you are waiting for these. People who expect a wedding prepare for it.

Without spot or blemish, and at peace. Be diligent, spoudasate, is the letter’s word for earnest, grace-driven effort (1:5, 10). Found, heurethēnai, picks up verse 10: everything will be found out, so be diligent about what is found in you. Without spot and blemish: like Christ, the spotless Lamb (1 Peter 1:19), and the opposite of the false teachers, who are blots and blemishes at the church’s own feast (2:13). At peace: with God through Christ (Romans 5:1), and with one another.

How can I be found without spot or blemish when I still sin? In two ways. First, by standing in Christ: his spotless righteousness is counted as yours, and his blood cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7). On that day you will be found in him, not having a righteousness of your own (Philippians 3:9). Second, by growing in holiness now, which is the fruit and evidence of being in him. Peter calls for diligence, not perfection. Keep short accounts with God, confess sin promptly, make peace with those you have wronged, and pursue holiness from a heart at rest in Christ’s finished work. He will present you blameless (Jude 24).

Count the patience of our Lord as salvation. Verse 9 as a command. The scoffers count it slowness; believers count it salvation. Every day Christ has not yet come is another day in which someone you love can still turn to him, and in which you yourself are being made ready (v. 14).

Our beloved brother Paul. These two men had a serious public disagreement at Antioch, where Paul opposed him to his face and later told the story in a letter the churches read (Galatians 2:11–14). Peter calls him beloved brother and commends his wisdom, inspired wisdom from God. There is no trace of the quarrel: that is what grace does to an old wound. Paul also taught that God’s patience leads to repentance (Romans 2:4).

Hard to understand. An honest admission from one apostle about another, and a small comfort to anyone who has struggled through Romans. Some of Paul’s teaching, perhaps on grace, freedom, election, or the last things, requires careful thought.

Twist to their own destruction. Ignorant, amatheis, is untaught; unstable, astēriktoi, not established, as in 2:14. Twist, streblousin, is to wrench, as on a rack. The false teachers twisted Paul’s teaching on grace into a licence for immorality (Romans 3:8; 6:1). Difficulty is not the cause of the twisting: the ignorant and unstable are, and they do it to the plain parts too.

The other Scriptures. Peter already counts Paul’s letters among the Scriptures, alongside the Old Testament. Many scholars see this as a sign of a later date, when Paul’s letters had been gathered into a collection. But Paul’s letters were copied and passed between churches in his own lifetime (Colossians 4:16), and Peter speaks only of the letters he knows. If, as this commentary holds, Peter wrote this, Paul was very likely still alive or, if the early tradition of his death under Nero is right, only lately martyred. Either way it is the New Testament recognising itself as Scripture.

How can I avoid twisting Scripture? Read whole passages, not isolated verses, and ask what the author meant to his first readers before asking what it means for you. Let clear passages interpret harder ones. Read with the church: good preaching, sound commentaries, and the confessions of faith keep you from private eccentricities. Be especially careful when an interpretation happens to excuse what you already wanted to do; that was exactly the false teachers’ method. And come to the Bible humbly, ready to be corrected by it rather than to use it.

What it does not mean. Hard to understand does not mean Scripture is unclear in its main message, or that ordinary believers cannot read it. The gospel is clear (Psalm 19:7). It means some passages require careful, humble study, and that we must not twist them to suit ourselves.

On a Tuesday. Is there someone with whom you are not at peace, perhaps a fellow believer who once rebuked you publicly, as Paul did Peter? Christ has made your peace with God, so follow Peter’s example: speak of them warmly, and seek peace.
verseByVerse.note: Peter already counts Paul’s letters among “the Scriptures.”

verseByVerse.quote: You therefore, beloved, knowing this beforehand, take care that you are not carried away with the error of lawless people and lose your own stability. But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Knowing this beforehand. Proginōskontes, being forewarned: the letter’s purpose in a phrase. Forewarning is itself the protection.

Take care that you are not carried away. Take care, phylassesthe, is a sentry’s word. Carried away, synapachthentes, is swept along, as by a crowd. It is the word Paul used of Barnabas being carried away by Peter’s hypocrisy at Antioch (Galatians 2:13). Peter knew from his own failure how easily a good man is swept along. Lawless, athesmōn, is the word used of the men of Sodom (2:7).

Lose your own stability. Stability, stērigmos, shares a root with established (1:12) and with the unstable souls baited and twisting Scripture (2:14; 3:16). Peter’s fear is that the steady will be pulled into that instability. And it is the word Jesus gave him: when you have turned again, strengthen (stērison) your brothers (Luke 22:32). His last sentence is still obeying that command.

But grow in the grace and knowledge. After two chapters of warning, the last command is unexpected. Grow, auxanete, is present tense: keep growing. Peter does not end by telling them to watch the heretics more closely; he tells them to get on with maturing. A tree that is growing is far harder to uproot than one being braced. Grace is God’s favour, known ever more deeply, because a man who forgets he was cleansed stops growing (1:9). Knowledge is personal knowledge of Christ (1:2–3, 8), reclaimed from the men peddling a counterfeit. The answer to false knowledge is not less knowledge but the real thing, and it is knowledge of a person. The letter ends where it began (1:2).

How do I actually grow in grace? Grace is not a substance you collect but the favour of God in Christ, known more deeply. You grow in it by using the means God has given: his word read, heard and preached; prayer; the Lord’s Supper and the fellowship of the church; and obedience, which opens the heart to know him more (John 14:21). You also grow through suffering and repentance, as each fresh sight of your need shows you more of his kindness. Growth is slow and often unseen, like a tree. Do not measure it day by day. Keep near the sources, and over years it will show.

What it does not mean. Lose your stability does not mean true believers can finally fall away. Peter has said they will never fall if they grow (1:10). The warning is one of God’s means to keep them standing.

To him be the glory. To Jesus Christ: a doxology offering him the glory due to God alone, who says, my glory I give to no other (Isaiah 42:8). It is a final testimony to his deity; the letter began by calling him our God and Saviour (1:1), and it ends by giving him God’s glory. Day of eternity, hēmera aiōnos, occurs nowhere else in the New Testament: a day that has no evening. If, as this commentary holds, Peter wrote them, these are the last recorded words of the man who denied his Lord in a courtyard, written when he knew his death was near.

For worship. The last word of Peter is glory, and the glory is Christ’s. The fisherman who sank in the waves, who cursed and swore that he did not know him, who was found and forgiven on a beach at dawn, ends his life giving that same Lord the glory that belongs to God alone. That is what grace does. To our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ be the glory, now, in the long patience of this age, and on the day of eternity that will never end. Amen.

3.theology:
The word of God and the uniform world: The scoffers claim that the world runs on unbroken natural regularity (v. 4). Peter points to two interruptions by the word of God, creation and the flood; the same word has spoken of a third, the fire.

Divine patience and salvation: Verse 9 says God is “not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.” Reformed theology reads it in its setting: he is patient “toward you”, the chosen community, and the delay is the time in which all who will repent are gathered. This is not universalism, for the day will still shut the door, nor does it contradict election: patience is the means by which the elect are gathered.

New creation as promise: The new heavens and new earth of verse 13 are the horizon of the whole letter. Herman Bavinck’s axiom, grace restores nature, applies here: the fire purifies creation rather than abolishing it, and the new creation is this creation glorified. Anthony Hoekema’s The Bible and the Future argues that the new earth is a renewal, not a replacement, which is why Christian hope is not escapism: the world we tend and serve matters, because it is the world God intends to redeem.
3.examples:
Then: The scoffers’ question, “Where is the promise of his coming?”, has been asked in every generation since the first believers died, and Peter’s answer stands: God’s patience is mercy.

Now: “What sort of people ought you to be” (v. 11) is the letter’s most searching question. A person who believes the day is coming lives with moral seriousness, urgency about the gospel, and longing for righteousness.
